1.4.src: World Bank, World Development Indicators — Food production index (2014-2016 = 100) - Egypt, Arab Rep. (AG.PRD.FOOD.XD)
1.4.note: FAO-compiled index; latest available reference year is 2022, series discontinued after 2022 in WDI. Next level not proposed: Level 4 would require the index to exceed 115. Egypt's published value of 109.1 (2022) falls 5.9 points short of that cut; no source in the retrieved pages reports an Egyptian food production index at or above 115 on the 2014-2016 base. (CEIC reports 124.98 for Egypt in 2016, but that is on the older 2004-2006=100 base and is therefore not comparable to this indicator's cut points, and CEIC is T5.). The quoted figure is exactly the WDI/FAO indicator AG.PRD.FOOD.XD, 'Food production index (2014-2016 = 100)', for Egypt, Arab Rep. Same base period and same definition as the indicator named in this cell. Corroborated by an independent T1 series (World Bank WDI AG.PRD.FOOD.XD): 109.07 for 2022.
1.4.tier_detail: FAO-compiled index; latest available reference year is 2022, series discontinued after 2022 in WDI

1.3.src: World Bank, World Development Indicators — Employment in agriculture (% of total employment) (modeled ILO estimate), Egypt, Arab Rep.
1.3.note: ILO modeled estimate (ILOEST) nowcast for 2025, not a directly observed survey figure; World Bank portal displays the value rounded to whole percent. Next level not proposed: Level 4 would require the agricultural employment share to have fallen below 15 percent of total employment. It has not: the ILO modeled 2025 value is 18 (17.52 unrounded on the same ILOSTAT series per the T5 aggregator), and the observed CAPMAS 2024 survey figure is higher still at 18.7 percent. Neither the modeled nor the survey-based measure is within three points of the 15 cut, and the series is declining by roughly half a point per year, so no published figure supports the next rung. The indicator name 'Employment in agriculture (%)' omits its denominator; the quoted series is explicitly '% of total employment', which is the standard reading. The series also covers ISIC-A (agriculture, hunting, forestry and fishing), i.e. slightly broader than agriculture alone — this is the open definitional question flagged in the indicator census. The reference-year 2025 figure is an ILO MODELLED nowcast rather than an observed labor force survey result. An observed national figure sits alongside it: CAPMAS's 2024 annual labor force survey, as reported by the State Information Service (T3), states 'Agriculture and fishing remained the largest employment sectors, engaging 5.594 million workers, representing 18.7 percent of the workforce' — consistent with the modeled 18 and confirming the modeled series is not drifting from national data. A commercial T5 aggregator (statbase.org) reproduces the same ILOSTAT series at 17.52 percent for 2025 and 17.98 for 2024, i.e. the unrounded value behind the World Bank's 18. An independent T1 series (World Bank WDI SL.AGR.EMPL.ZS (ILO modeled estimate)) reports 17.52 for 2025, which differs from the value recorded here.
1.3.tier_detail: ILO modelled estimate (ILOEST) nowcast for 2025, not a directly observed survey figure; World Bank portal displays the value rounded to whole percent

1.2.src: World Bank, World Development Indicators — Cereal yield (kg per hectare), Egypt, Arab Rep. (AG.YLD.CREL.KG)
1.2.note: Next level not proposed: Not required: level 5 is the top rung and the published value of 7402 kg/ha lies above the highest cut point of 6000. The World Bank indicator AG.YLD.CREL.KG is precisely 'Cereal yield (kg per hectare)', sourced from FAO production data (FAOSTAT QCL), national-level, covering wheat, rice, maize, barley, oats, rye, millet, sorghum, buckwheat and mixed grains harvested for dry grain. This matches the named construct exactly; no rural/national or crop-subset mismatch arises. Corroborated by an independent T1 series (World Bank WDI AG.YLD.CREL.KG): 7402.2 for 2023.

1.1.src: World Bank, World Development Indicators — Agriculture, forestry, and fishing, value added per worker (constant 2015 US$) [NV.AGR.EMPL.KD]
1.1.note: Denominator (agricultural employment) is an ILO modeled estimate; WDI metadata notes 'Data on employment are modeled estimates by the International Labor Organization (ILO) ILOSTAT database.'. Next level not proposed: Level 5 was not proposed because the published value, 8,942.42 constant 2015 US$, falls short of the 10000 cut point by roughly 1,058 dollars. No source in the retrieved pages publishes an Egypt figure at or above 10000 for this construct on any price basis or any reference year; the Arab World aggregate does exceed 10000 (10,945.1 in 2025) but that is a regional aggregate, not Egypt, and cannot be substituted. Should the definition be ratified as current US$ rather than constant 2015 US$, the level could move, but no current-US$ per-worker figure for Egypt was found in these pages. The indicator name reads 'Agriculture value added per worker (USD)'. The published series actually retrieved is WDI NV.AGR.EMPL.KD, whose long definition covers 'Agriculture, forestry, and fishing ... ISIC (Rev. 4) divisions 01-03' and is denominated in constant 2015 US$, not current USD. So the evidence sits on the broader-scope, constant-price side of the unratified definitional question: sector scope is wider than 'agriculture' alone (it includes forestry and fishing), and the price basis is a 2015 constant-dollar series rather than the bare 'USD' the name implies. The current-US$ counterpart (NV.AGR.TOTL.CD divided by employment) is not published as a per-worker series in these pages, so no alternative figure on the narrower reading exists here. Figure is national for Egypt, which is what the indicator asks for. Corroborated by an independent T1 series (World Bank WDI NV.AGR.EMPL.KD): 8942.42 for 2025.
1.1.tier_detail: Denominator (agricultural employment) is an ILO modelled estimate; WDI metadata notes 'Data on employment are modeled estimates by the International Labour Organization (ILO) ILOSTAT database.'

1.5.value: DATA GAP — Started with the T1 CAPMAS pages (Sources 1-5): the annual bulletins on production, foreign trade and availability for consumption define الفاقد (losses during sorting, packing, transport, storage, processing) as a term in the food-balance identity and publish self-sufficiency ratios, per-capita availability and food-gap figures, but the retrieved text contains no loss percentage - dead end for a national rate. Then Source 6 (MDPI Sustainability, wheat value chain, ICARDA/ARC): only quantified Egypt figure found, 20.62% of wheat supply lost or wasted, but scoped to wheat and to loss-plus-waste. Source 7 (ScienceDirect, wheat/water) returned a Cloudflare captcha page with no data. Source 8 (Foods 2017, Kumar & Kalita) is a global developing-country review with no Egypt-specific rate in the retrieved text. Source 9 (COMCEC/NRI presentation, T5) is the only source addressing Egyptian cereal post-harvest losses directly, and it states the literature is limited, gives a 16-48% range from 1970s work, notes APHLIS does not cover North Africa, and applies a 10% guesstimate - a T5 tier that cannot carry a statistic in any case. No FAO Food Loss Index or FAOSTAT loss-percentage page for Egypt was among the supplied sources.
1.5.note: Wheat-only value-chain study combining loss and waste; denominator includes imported wheat. Secondary range figure comes from a conference presentation citing 1970s literature and an explicit 'guesstimate'. Next level not proposed: Nothing in the retrieved pages reports an all-crop, harvest-to-market loss percentage for Egypt separated from consumption-stage waste, and no national statistical office or FAO/FLI country estimate for Egypt appears in the supplied set; without that, even level 1 would rest on a construct the sources do not measure. The indicator name asserts an all-crop national post-harvest loss rate. The best available Egyptian figure (20.62%) is (i) wheat only, not all crops; (ii) loss AND wastage across the full life cycle, so it includes retail and household food waste that falls outside 'post-harvest loss'; and (iii) computed over total supply including imports rather than over domestic harvested production. The COMCEC/NRI case study (T5) states for Egyptian cereals: 'Limited published literature on postharvest losses in Egypt. Literature from 1970's suggests a range of 16-48%' and that the authors 'made a guesstimate' of 10% postharvest loss for wheat, maize and rice - again cereals only, and self-described as a guess. CAPMAS bulletins define a loss term (الفاقد, quantities lost during sorting, packing, transport, storage and processing) inside the food-balance identity but the retrieved pages carry no percentage for it.

1.6.value: DATA GAP — 1) Checked the two T1 official-statistics routes first: FAO Microdata catalog entry for Egypt's 2009-2010 Agricultural Census — scope list covers holdings characteristics, area, irrigation, employment, machinery and livestock, with no marketing or sales-channel item; CAPMAS NADA Agriculture collection (47 studies) and the Annual Bulletin of Cooperative Activity in Agricultural Sector 2016/2017 front matter — the bulletin covers cooperative numbers, members, capital, loans and 'marketing' services by governorate, but the retrieved text is preface/index only with no smallholder market-access rate. 2) Went to the peer-reviewed/analytical tier: Tabe-Ojong & Abay (AgEcon Search PDF) and its RePEc listing — construct is participation in contract farming/high-value chains among irrigated smallholders, no national access percentage in the retrieved text. 3) Checked government artifacts: MALR PRIME project page — outputs only (42 thousand acres of marketing contracts, 256 marketing committees, 7 governorates). 4) Checked grey literature: GIZ Gender Value Chain Assessment 2023 (contents list flags 'Market Access' and a 'Selling point' figure for a 100-farmer Minya/Beni Suef sample, values not in retrieved text) and GIZ AIP industrial scan 2022 (qualitative factors affecting inclusive procurement, six governorates, no rate). Dead ends: no FAOSTAT/WDI/RuLIS indicator on formal-market participation surfaced; no national household or farm survey table on channel of sale was among the supplied pages. Concluded found=false with abstain hold.
1.6.note: Next level not proposed: Even the lowest rung (below the 20 cut) is withheld because the evidence does not establish any measured share of Egyptian smallholders with formal-market access — not a low one and not a high one. The specific missing item is a nationally representative survey or official statistic reporting the proportion of Egyptian smallholders selling through formal channels (contracts, cooperatives, registered wholesale/export buyers, organised retail); no such published proportion appears in the supplied material. Indicator name asserts national smallholder ACCESS to formal markets, expressed as a percentage. The best available Egyptian evidence in these pages is Tabe-Ojong & Abay (IFPRI), 'Smallholder farmers' participation in profitable value chains and contract farming: Evidence from irrigated agriculture in Egypt', which estimates a multivariate probit of joint PARTICIPATION in value chains and contract farming among a survey sample of irrigated smallholders — participation in one contractual channel is not the same as access to formal markets, and the sample is regional (irrigated governorates), not national. Its only quotable general statement is that participation 'remains low in Africa', which is a continental, not Egyptian, claim. Contextual non-matching material: GIZ AIP industrial scan (T4) describes willingness of buyers to source from smallholders in six Upper Egypt governorates qualitatively with no rate; MALR's PRIME page (T3) reports programme outputs — 'Implementing marketing contracts for 42 thousand acres' and 'Forming 256 marketing committees for the small farmers' in seven governorates — which are project counts, not a share of smallholders with market access; GIZ Gender Value Chain Assessment lists a 'Selling point' figure for a 100-farmer Minya/Beni Suef sample, again neither national nor a published access percentage. None of these can substitute for the named construct.

1.7.value: DATA GAP — Worked through the ten supplied pages in tier order. (1) CAPMAS censusinfo bulletin on investment loans to farmers — read fully; it reports totals in billion pounds by loan maturity, with the extracted text's digits largely stripped; no farmer counts or percentages. (2) and (3) CAPMAS Annual Bulletin of agricultural sector cooperative activity 2016/17 and 2017/18 — read prefaces and full table indexes; every loan table is 'value of in-kind and in cash loans granted ... and the benefitted areas', i.e. money and feddans by governorate, plus association membership counts; no table promises borrowers as a share of farmers. (4) CAPMAS agriculture subject landing page — navigation shell only, no data. (5) CAPMAS Zemam and agricultural ownership bulletin overview — land area and ownership metadata, no credit variable. (6) FAO World Census of Agriculture, Egypt 1999/2000 — checked for a credit or 'holdings reporting credit' block; the extract covers holdings, tenure, employment, land use, crops, livestock and machinery, but contains no credit item; noted the 4,541,884 holdings figure only as a potential denominator. (7) ScienceDirect 'Agricultural credit constraints in smallholder farming' — blocked by captcha, nothing readable, dead end. (8) and (9) Ministry of Environment CLEI green-finance pages for the Agricultural Bank of Egypt (English and Arabic) — full product catalog with amounts, tenors and interest rates; supply-side terms only, no uptake or coverage share. (10) Forbes Middle East on Egypt's farm credit — T5, reports CAPMAS investment-loan totals of EGP 56 billion for FY2023-24; useful context but a T5 page may not carry a statistic and in any case reports value, not farmer share. Searched all pages for the words 'percent', '%', 'share of farmers' and 'access to credit' in the credit context; the only percentages present are interest rates, financing ratios (80%, 25-70% of production costs) and year-on-year growth rates. Conclusion: the named construct is not published in any supplied page for Egypt.
1.7.note: Next level not proposed: No level, including level 1, is supported: the evidence does not establish any measured share of Egyptian farmers with agricultural credit access, only loan values, loan product terms, and benefitted cultivated area. Level 1 would require a published figure below 10 percent for the named construct, and no such figure appears in the supplied pages. The indicator names a SHARE OF FARMERS with credit ACCESS. The best Egypt evidence in the supplied pages is (a) CAPMAS annual bulletins of agricultural cooperative activity, which tabulate the VALUE of in-kind and cash loans granted by season and governorate and the benefitted AREA (feddans), not the number or share of farmers served; (b) Forbes Middle East reporting CAPMAS figures that investment loans to farmers and agribusiness rose to EGP 56 billion in FY2023-24 — again a monetary total; (c) a Ministry of Environment green-finance page listing Agricultural Bank of Egypt product terms (e.g. crop loans of EGP 2,000–10,000 for small farmers), which describes supply-side offer, not uptake or coverage. Separately, the census note for this row flags that Egypt's previously recorded figure came from Findex-style 'rural adults aged 15+' borrowing, which is both a different population (includes non-farmers) and a different concept (borrowing/use rather than access); no such Findex page was supplied here either, so it cannot be quote-verified. The FAO World Census of Agriculture page for Egypt 1999/2000 gives 4,541,884 holdings, which would be a plausible denominator but the supplied pages contain no matching count of credit-receiving farmers, so no ratio can be formed.

1.8.value: DATA GAP — Reviewed all nine supplied pages in order. FAO SHARP+ project page (T1): only a forward-looking target of 8,000 farmers by 2027, no adoption share. FAO family-farming page: blocked by Cloudflare, no content. Scientific Reports / PMC mirror of Swelam et al. 2026 (seven governorates, 2953 farmers): abstract and introduction only in the retrieved text; qualitative 'limited uptake', no adoption percentage in the supplied portion. FAO Knowledge Repository record for 'Toward climate-smart agriculture in Egypt' (2022): catalog record and synopsis only — practice case studies, no adoption statistic on the page supplied (the 92-page PDF itself was not retrieved). Kassem et al. 2019 (Delta Nile, 792 farmers): gives 51.9% with no knowledge of climate change — awareness, not practice adoption, and only two governorates. ICARDA/AFESD raised-bed report: table of contents lists wheat area under mechanised raised beds in Sharkia, but the retrieved text contains only table titles and the executive summary, no percentage values. ScienceDirect item: captcha wall, no content. Exa library page (T5): abstract of an economic analysis with emissions shares, no adoption rate, and tier-5 material cannot carry a statistic in any case. Dead ends: two of nine pages were access-blocked; no FAOSTAT, CAPMAS, Ministry of Agriculture and Land Reclamation, or World Bank indicator page carrying a farmer-level CSA adoption share for Egypt was among the supplied sources.
1.8.note: Next level not proposed: Not applicable — no level proposed. The specific missing item is any nationally scoped, farmer-denominated adoption rate for a defined set of climate-smart practices in Egypt, from a statistical office, FAO/World Bank database, or nationally representative survey. Closest evidence: (a) Kassem et al. 2019 (Sustainability, via DigitalCommons@USU) surveyed 792 farmers in two Nile Delta governorates and reports that 51.9% had NO knowledge of the climate change phenomenon, with manure use, changed crop patterns and crop rotation the commonest adaptation measures among the aware minority — this is an awareness statistic for two governorates, not a national share of farmers using climate-smart practices; (b) Swelam et al. 2026 (Sci Rep, 2953 farmers, seven governorates) reports qualitatively 'limited uptake of technical adaptation measures' concentrated on 'low-cost, incremental practices' with modern irrigation and digital tools 'rarely adopted' — no adoption percentage is given; (c) the ICARDA/AFESD technical report tabulates the 'Relative Importance of Wheat Areas under MRB Farming in Sharkia Governorate' — a share of AREA under one practice in one governorate, which is the exact land-vs-farmers, single-practice, sub-national mismatch flagged in the indicator census; (d) the FAO SHARP+ project page states a forward-looking target that 'over 8,000 farmers will adopt climate-smart agriculture and biodiversity-friendly practices across 3,000 hectares' by 2027 — a project target, not a denominator-based national share. Egypt has roughly 4-5 million agricultural holders, so 8,000 is not convertible to a meaningful national percentage.

8.1.src: World Bank Open Data (WDI), Prevalence of undernourishment (% of population) — Egypt, Arab Rep. (source: FAO)
8.1.note: FAO model-based estimate derived from food balance sheets and household consumption distributions; World Bank portal displays the figure rounded to whole percent (the underlying FAO series value for 2023 is reported elsewhere as 9.4). Next level not proposed: Level 4 would require a prevalence below 7.5 percent. Egypt's published 2023 value is 9 (9.4 in the finer-grained FAO series shown on TheGlobalEconomy's reproduction), which is above 7.5, and the series on the World Bank page is rising rather than falling toward that cut (the y-axis on the Egypt chart runs to 10.0 and the most recent value is the series maximum). Nothing in the supplied pages shows an Egyptian PoU figure under 7.5 for any recent year. The World Bank series SN.ITK.DEFC.ZS is FAO's SDG indicator 2.1.1, prevalence of undernourishment as a percentage of the national population — exactly the named construct, for Egypt, Arab Rep. An independent T1 series (World Bank WDI SN.ITK.DEFC.ZS) reports 9.4 for 2023, which differs from the value recorded here.
8.1.tier_detail: FAO model-based estimate derived from food balance sheets and household consumption distributions; World Bank portal displays the figure rounded to whole percent (the underlying FAO series value for 2023 is reported elsewhere as 9.4)

8.5.value: DATA GAP — Worked through the ten supplied pages in tier order. Source 1 and Source 2 (CAPMAS censusinfo, T1, Agricultural Property and Rein 2017 and 2015): catalog landing pages listing downloadable press releases, a bulletin and tables, but the retrieved text contains no sex-disaggregated ownership values - the underlying PDFs were not supplied. Source 4 (CAPMAS Arabic 'zemam and agricultural ownership' bulletin overview, T1): abstract and keywords cover total zemam, government and private lands and 'المساحة المملوكة' (owned area), but the unit of analysis is stated as feddans and no gender breakdown appears; this is the most likely home for an Egyptian owner-based figure and is the gap to close on a rerun. Source 3 (FAO microdata, Egypt Agricultural Census 2009-2010, T1): methodology metadata only; scope lists holding characteristics and employment, no published results table. Source 5 (FAO Gender and Land Rights Database, T1): the deep link returned a 404 error page, so the GLRD Egypt country profile - the natural custodian for this indicator - could not be read. Source 6 (FAOSTAT structural data from agricultural censuses, T1): confirms the domain disseminates 'sex of agricultural holders' as a percentage of holdings, but the catalog page itself carries no Egypt value; the actual data download was not fetched. Source 7 (FAO/CIHEAM/CIRAD small-scale family farming in Egypt, T2): the retrieved text stops at the table of contents, which lists '1.2.6 Gender composition of the holders' on page 20 - the figure is very likely there but is not in the text supplied, so quoting it would be fabrication. Source 8 (FAO Country Gender Assessment of the Agriculture and Rural Sector: Egypt, T2): retrieved text is front matter plus the opening of 'Main findings', all qualitative on invisibility and structural barriers; no land-ownership percentage in the supplied extract. Source 9 (GIZ Gender Value Chain Assessment, T4): the list of figures includes 'Figure 2: Land ownership by gender', but this is a 100-farmer purposive sample in Minya and Beni Suef, i.e. sub-national and non-representative even if the numbers had been supplied, which they were not. Source 10 (GLTN Arab Land Initiative presentation, T5): the only page carrying an actual Egypt number - 212779 female holders, 4 percent - rejected on tier and on the holder-versus-owner construct as set out in construct_note. Dead ends: no SDG 5.a.1 reporting, no Demographic and Health Survey asset-ownership module, and no CAPMAS ownership tabulation by sex appeared among the retrieved pages.
8.5.note: Next level not proposed: No level was proposed at all, so no next rung applies. The specific missing item is a T1-T4 published figure, for Egypt, for the share of land OWNERS (or landholding-title holders) who are women - or, failing that, an admissible-tier restatement of the census holder share that the assessment could ratify as a proxy after resolving the owner-versus-holder definitional question. Context only, not recorded as the cell value: a T5 slide deck ('Women's land rights in Arab countries', GLTN Arab Land Initiative) tabulates FAO World Programme for the Census of Agriculture 2010 results giving Egypt (census 2009/2012) 5401432 total holders, of whom 212779 (4%) are female holders operating 114694 ha (3%) of area. Two problems sit on top of each other. First, tier: the page is T5, which is admissible for existence facts but never for a statistic, so this number cannot be ratified from the evidence supplied. Second, construct: 'holder' is defined on that same page, per Eurostat, as the person on whose account and in whose name the holding is operated and who bears the economic risk - the holder 'can own the holding outright or rent it or be a hereditary long-term leaseholder or a usufructuary or a trustee'. That is operatorship, not ownership. The indicator as NAMED asks for women who OWN land, so the canonical holder statistic sits on the wrong side of the unratified definitional question flagged in the indicator census. A ratified owner-based figure would need to come from a land-ownership or asset-ownership survey (e.g. SDG 5.a.1, or CAPMAS agricultural property/'zemam' ownership tabulations), none of which are present in numeric form in the retrieved pages.

2.4.src: World Bank World Development Indicators — Individuals using the Internet (% of population), Egypt, Arab Rep. (source: ITU World Telecommunication/ICT Indicators Database)
2.4.note: World Bank portal displays the ITU figure rounded to whole percent; underlying ITU estimate may carry decimals. Next level not proposed: Level 5 would require a published figure above 80%. The most recent ITU/World Bank value for Egypt is 75, five points below the 80 cut; the only other national evidence in the supplied pages (MCIT ICT Indicators in Brief, 72.2% internet penetration for 2021/2022) is lower still, and no admissible source in these pages reports Egyptian individual internet use above 80%. The World Bank/ITU series 'Individuals using the Internet (% of population)' is exactly the named construct, national population basis, for Egypt, Arab Rep. Note the national MCIT survey-based figure of 72.2% internet penetration for 2021/2022 (T3, ICT Indicators in Brief, September 2023) is an earlier-year national figure and is consistent in magnitude. Corroborated by an independent T1 series (World Bank WDI IT.NET.USER.ZS): 74.65 for 2024.
2.4.tier_detail: World Bank portal displays the ITU figure rounded to whole percent; underlying ITU estimate may carry decimals

2.1.value: DATA GAP — 1) ITU DataHub Egypt country page for 'Population coverage, by mobile network technology' (i=100095) — returns national-only series for at least 2G/3G/LTE/5G; no rural/urban selector in the retrieved page. 2) ITU Facts and Figures 2025 'Mobile network coverage' chapter — contains the urban/rural narrative but only at world, income-group, region, LDC/LLDC/SIDS level; Egypt is not named. 3) ITU Statistics landing page — confirms an urban/rural coverage time series exists but only 'for the world, by geographic regions, by urban/rural area and by level of development', i.e. aggregates, not countries. 4) ITU Measuring Digital Development 2025 and 2023 PDFs and Facts and Figures 2020 PDF — front matter and regional charts only; no Egypt rural coverage value in the retrieved text. 5) ITU estimation-methods document — confirms 'Percentage of the population covered by mobile networks (at least 3G, at least LTE/4G)' is modeled at national level; no rural variant documented. 6) MCIT ICT Indicators in Brief September 2023 and the MCIT Indicators index (T3, the national regulator/ministry) — mobile penetration, mobile Internet users, ADSL by governorate group, and 'Number of Local Exchanges in Rural Areas' (fixed, not mobile broadband); no rural mobile broadband coverage figure. 7) nPerf coverage map — T5 crowdsourced, no quotable statistic and inadmissible for a prerequisite row. Dead end on the named construct.
2.1.note: ITU country coverage values are operator-reported/modeled national estimates with no urban-rural disaggregation published at country level. Next level not proposed: Not applicable in the usual sense because no level is claimed; the specific gap is that no source states what share of Egypt's RURAL population is within range of a 3G or 4G signal. Even level 1 cannot be evidenced, since level 1 would also require a rural figure (below 20) that no publisher has produced. The indicator names RURAL coverage. The best available Egypt-specific evidence is NATIONAL: ITU DataHub reports for Egypt, 2025, 'At least 3G 99.8%', 'At least LTE/WiMAX 98%', 'At least 2G 99.9%', 'At least 5G 11%' (% of individuals). These are whole-population figures and cannot be read as rural coverage: ITU's own 2025 Facts and Figures shows that the uncovered residual is 'exclusively rural', so a national figure systematically overstates the rural value by construction. This cell therefore sits on the wrong side of the census's open question: recording the ITU national at-least-3G number here would mechanically score level 5 for a rural construct that no source has measured for Egypt. ITU's global/regional rural numbers (e.g. 4G covering 84 per cent of rural areas worldwide; Arab States 5G 13 per cent) are aggregates, not Egypt values, and rule 5 forbids importing them.

2.5.value: DATA GAP — 1) ITU ICT prices landing page (itu.int/en/ITU-D/Statistics/Pages/ICTprices) — confirms the 2025 collection, the four baskets and links to country-level 2008-2025 Excel downloads, but carries no country values in text. 2) ITU DataHub IPB dashboard filtered to Egypt (datahub.itu.int and beta.datahub.itu.int, ?e=EGY) — both returned navigation shells plus the indicator picker listing the four baskets; no rendered data. 3) beta.datahub.itu.int/data/?e=EGY&i=100122 ('Current ICT price baskets') — same, only the fixed-broadband basket definition text, no numbers. 4) ITU 'Measuring digital development: The affordability of ICT services 2024' PDF — supplied text stops at the foreword/contents; contains the Broadband Commission 2 %-of-monthly-GNI target language but no Egypt row. 5) ITU ICT Price Basket Statistics Manual 2025 — methodology only, confirms basket definitions and the retirement/legacy status of the 2021-2024 high-consumption definition; no country data. 6) Legacy ITU IPB page (itu.int/ITU-D/ict/ipb) — 2008/2010 composite IPB, wrong construct (composite of fixed telephone, mobile cellular and fixed broadband) and no Egypt figure. 7) World Bank ITIDA ICT indicators report (openknowledge) — indicator-methodology gap analysis for Egypt, no price basket value. 8) Scribd copy of the Egypt Digital Economy Country Assessment — T5 host, only front matter and contents captured, no price figure. Dead end: none of the retrieved pages exposes the Excel/API payload that carries Egypt's basket percentages.
2.5.note: Retrieved pages are client-side-rendered dashboards; the underlying data table did not render into the captured text. Next level not proposed: Level 1 (value below 10 % of GNI pc) is not proposed because the supplied sources contain no Egypt data point whatsoever — only dashboard chrome, basket-name menu labels, and methodology text. Assigning any level would require importing a number from outside the evidence set. The indicator name 'Mobile broadband price (% GNI pc)' does not fix the basket. The supplied ITU pages confirm that from the 2025 collection ITU publishes at least three candidate mobile series for each economy — 'Data-only mobile broadband basket 5 GB, as a % of GNI pc', 'Mobile broadband data and voice low-consumption basket total (70 min, 50 SMS, 1 GB), as a % of monthly GNI per capita', and 'Mobile broadband data and voice high-consumption basket total (140 min, 20 SMS, 5 GB), % GNI p.c.' — and that the pre-2025 methodology (in force 2021-2024, with the 2GB data-only basket) has been retired to a legacy/temporary-collection status ('Temporary data collection: The Mobile-broadband data and voice high-consumption basket, according to the 2021-2024 definition'). Any Egypt value must therefore be tagged with which of these baskets it comes from before it can be compared with another country's value; the census's open question is confirmed by these sources but not resolved by them. Note also that ITU's denominator convention here is MONTHLY GNI per capita (the Broadband Commission target is 'entry-level broadband services costing less than 2 per cent of monthly GNI per capita'), whereas the indicator name says only '% GNI pc'.

2.7.value: DATA GAP — 1) CAPMAS microdata catalog (censusinfo.capmas.gov.eg), EGY-CAPMAS-BEIMIS-2011 'Basic ICT Indicators for Measuring the Information Society (Household) 2011' — checked the F1 (Telecommunications) and F8 (General Indicators) data dictionaries and two variable pages (V13, V17). The file carries r_u_code (urban/rural) and 'mobile' / 'mobile_no' variables, but no smartphone variable, and the published category tables are unweighted record counts with an explicit non-representativeness warning. Dead end for the named construct. 2) The 2006/2011 questionnaire PDF (download/592) — contains a household question on third-generation-enabled mobiles and mobile internet use, but is an instrument, not results, and carries no rural tabulation. Dead end. 3) MCIT 'ICT Indicators in Brief', September 2023 and January 2020 (T3) — national mobile penetration, subscriptions, mobile internet users, ADSL regional distribution; the only rural entry is the count of local exchanges in rural areas. No rural smartphone ownership. Dead end. 4) World Bank/ITIDA RTA report on ICT indicators (T2, openknowledge) — a methodology and gap-analysis document; it discusses indicator categories and gaps, not values. Dead end. 5) IFPRI/CGIAR policy note 'Digital Agricultural Technology in Egypt: Insights from App Developers' (T2) — qualitative; references smartphone proliferation and gaps in digital access but publishes no rural ownership rate. Dead end. 6) Ahram Online report of CAPMAS HIECS 2015 (T5) — the only page with a rural smartphone number (13.9% of rural families). Recorded as context in construct_note; not ratifiable as a statistic at T5, and a household rather than individual measure. Not searched/retrieved and worth a future pass: the CAPMAS HIECS 2019/2021 durable-goods tables, the CAPMAS 'ICT Access and Use by Households and Individuals Survey 2021/2022' full report (cited in the MCIT brief for the 72.2% internet penetration figure and likely to carry urban/rural splits), and the GSMA Consumer Survey country data for Egypt.

Next level not proposed: What is missing for any level above withheld: a CAPMAS, ITU, GSMA Consumer Survey or Findex table that reports, for Egypt, the share of rural respondents (individuals) who own a smartphone, published by the statistical office or an admissible T1-T4 publisher and quotable from the page itself. Nothing in the retrieved pages disaggregates smartphone ownership by rural residence at an admissible tier; the MCIT briefs stop at national subscription counts and the CAPMAS metadata pages stop at unweighted variable frequencies for the 2011 survey. Context only, not ratified: the Ahram Online report of the CAPMAS 2015 Household Income, Expenditure and Consumption Survey states that in rural areas 13.9 percent of families own smartphones (versus 31.7 percent urban and 22.1 percent nationally). Two mismatches with the indicator as named: (a) it is the share of rural HOUSEHOLDS owning at least one smartphone, not the share of rural INDIVIDUALS owning a personal smartphone — exactly the open definitional question the indicator census flags, and the household measure reads systematically higher than the individual one; (b) the publisher of the page carrying the number is a news outlet (T5), which is not an admissible tier for a statistic. The MCIT 'ICT Indicators in Brief' pages (T3) carry only national mobile subscription and penetration series (e.g. mobile penetration 98.34% and 105.01 million subscriptions in August 2023) with no rural/urban disaggregation and no smartphone-specific ownership measure; the only rural item there is 'Number of Local Exchanges in Rural Areas' (1072), a fixed-line infrastructure count.

3.8.value: Egypt has soil-mapping artifacts rather than a documented operating national digital soil information service: the Ministry of Agriculture and Land Reclamation told the Cabinet in May 2024 that it has adopted and applies
3.8.src: Egyptian Cabinet (رئاسة مجلس الوزراء) — رئيس الوزراء يناقش مقترح إنشاء منظومة رقمية لكافة الأراضي الزراعية على مستوي الجمهورية

The only 2024 government description is a single sentence in a meeting readout with no coverage, platform or access detail, and that same meeting was convened precisely because a comprehensive digital system for all agricultural land does not yet exist — the Cabinet directed the Future of Egypt Authority to hold a coordination meeting on linking existing agricultural systems with a newly proposed one, and the Future of Egypt executive described the proposal as addressing gaps in data available in currently applied systems. quality_evidence is empty because no evaluation, audit or performance report on any Egyptian soil map/database was retrieved; scale_evidence is empty because no coverage area, profile count, user count or geographic spread for a national soil database was published in these sources (the 5.6 million holdings figure in the same readout is the farmer-card holdings registry, not soil data). The indicator's unratified question — digitized legacy paper map versus operating digital soil information service — is answered on the weaker side by this evidence. The FAO paper (T2) documents "the production of digital soil and terrain data of Egypt in cooperation with the FAO and the European Soil Bureau (ESB)" by NARSS, i.e. a legacy digital soil and terrain dataset compiled in the 1990s, not an operating service. 4.7.note: Best available figure is a survey-based (Global Findex/ID4D 2021) estimate of national-ID-card ownership, a different construct from digital ID; ID4D digital-capability series for Egypt are binary flags, not coverage rates. Next level not proposed: Not applicable — no level proposed. The specific missing item is any published percentage, from a T1-T3 publisher, of Egyptians (or Egyptian adults) enrolled in or holding a digital identity credential capable of digital verification or online authentication. Until the indicator definition is ratified as either (a) foundational national-ID ownership or (b) ID4D's digital-identity capability series, the cell cannot be filled without misrepresenting the source. The indicator as named asks for digital ID coverage as a percentage. The ID4D DataBank page for Egypt (2021 column) reports 'ID ownership, total (% of population ages 15+)' at 87.4, with rural 87.2, urban 87.8, female 76.7 and male 98.5 — these are foundational national-ID-card ownership rates among adults 15+, i.e. possession of a credential, not evidence that the credential is digital or usable for digital authentication. On the same page ID4D's digital-capability series for Egypt read 'Digital data use (1 = yes; 0 = no)' 1.0, 'Digital ID verification (1 = yes; 0 = no)' 0.0 and 'Online digital identity (1 = yes; 0 = no)' 0.0 — binary system-level flags with no denominator, so they cannot be expressed as a percentage. This is precisely the open question flagged in the indicator census: the recorded Egypt value sits on the foundational-ownership side, while the digital-ID side exists and is unused, and it is on a % of adults 15+ denominator that is not comparable to other countries' denominators. Contextually, MCIT (T3) reports the Digital Egypt platform user base at 10.7 million in 2025 and states that only a 'pilot version of a digital identity verification application was developed', which corroborates that no operating population-wide digital ID with a published coverage rate exists. An independent T1 series (World Bank WDI ID.OWN.TOTL.ZS (World Bank Identification for Development (ID4D))) reports 98.78 for 2024.

4.9.value: DATA GAP — Reviewed all five supplied pages in order. (1) OECD Working Paper No. 35, 'Integrated Governance for Coherent Implementation of the SDGs in Egypt' (T2): the retrieved text covers foreword and acknowledgements and frames institutional/decision-making arrangements for SDGs generally; no agricultural or digital-agriculture coordination body appears in the retrieved extract. (2) OECD 'SME and Entrepreneurship Policy in Egypt', ch. 4 on strategic framework and delivery arrangements (T2): coordination discussion is confined to SME policy and MSMEDA. (3) MPED news item on the national statistics strategy (T3): records collaboration with 18 ministries on statistics development and mentions a 'Ministerial Group for Entrepreneurship' in the sidebar — neither is an agriculture/digital-agriculture mechanism. (4) MOIC page on Egypt–UNSDCF technical coordination meetings (T3): describes the Joint Steering Committee and five results groups (human capital; sustainable and inclusive economic development; climate resilience; governance; women's empowerment) — no agriculture or digital-agriculture results group. (5) PARIS21 National Statistical System Assessment of Egypt 2015 (tagged T5 by domain): notes weakening of statistical coordination mechanisms and lists a Consultancy Committee for Statistical Planning and Coordination — a statistics body, not an agricultural one, and in any case dated and not at an admissible tier for this prerequisite row. Dead ends: no Ministry of Agriculture and Land Reclamation, MCIT, or Cabinet decree text was among the retrieved pages, so the sector-specific instruments that would settle this cell (a digital-agriculture steering committee, an agri-data governance council, or an MALR–MCIT joint committee) could not be checked. Holding for ratification pending retrieval of MALR/MCIT/Cabinet sources.
4.9.note: Next level not proposed: 'Announced' or higher was not proposed because no retrieved page names any inter-ministerial committee, council, or standing coordination mechanism covering agriculture or agricultural digitalisation in Egypt. 'Absent' was likewise not proposed because the retrieved set contains no agriculture or digital-agriculture governance artifact whose silence could be read as evidence of non-existence. The closest retrieved items are: (a) the OECD working paper on integrated governance for SDG implementation in Egypt, which assesses whole-of-government institutional and decision-making arrangements for the SDGs rather than any agriculture or digital-agriculture coordination body; (b) the OECD SME and Entrepreneurship Policy in Egypt chapter on 'policy co-ordination mechanisms and delivery arrangements', which is explicitly about SME policy, not agriculture; (c) the Ministry of Planning page describing a national statistics strategy prepared 'in collaboration with 18 Egyptian ministries', which is a statistical-system process, not a standing agricultural coordination body; and (d) the MOIC page on the Egypt–UNSDCF Joint Steering Committee co-chaired by MPED and the UN Resident Coordinator with results groups co-chaired by line ministries — a UN development-cooperation governance structure, not a domestic inter-ministerial mechanism for agriculture or agricultural data. On the census's open question (standing body vs. any documented recurring mechanism), the UNSDCF steering committee would sit on the permissive side of that line, but it fails on sector: none of its five results groups is an agriculture or digital-agriculture group, so it does not evidence the named construct regardless of how the definition is ratified.

5.3.value: DATA GAP — 1) World Bank WDI page for SE.TER.ENRR, Egypt: found 'Egypt, Arab Rep. 2025 38' — total tertiary GER, all fields, not STEM; the page's 'Also Show' list offers only female/male splits and attainment series, no field-of-study breakdown. 2) UNESCO IESALC Higher Education Policy Observatory Egypt profile: gives 'GER, both sexes (%): 38.0%' — same all-fields construct, and the domain is not an admissible tier for a statistic in any case. 3) CAPMAS microdata catalog entry DDI-Egy-capmas-enrolled2024 (English and Arabic overviews and related-materials pages): the scope notes list tables by institution type, university and gender, and by 'theoretical and practical faculties', but no ISCED field-of-study or STEM aggregate, and no ratio to population. 4) CAPMAS press releases for 2022/2023 and 2023/2024: headcounts and theoretical/practical shares only. Dead end: no page retrieved carries a STEM gross enrollment ratio for Egypt, so found=false and the cell is held.
5.3.note: Context figure is all-fields tertiary GER from UIS administrative reporting; the underlying WDI page rounds values to whole percent and its most recent Egypt observation is dated 2025. Next level not proposed: No level, including level 1, can be evidenced: the retrieved pages contain no Egyptian STEM-field enrollment expressed as a percentage of any age cohort, so there is nothing to compare against the 10/20/30/40 cut points. What is missing specifically is a UIS or CAPMAS table of tertiary enrollment in ISCED fields 05-07 (natural sciences, ICT, engineering) divided by the relevant five-year age population. The indicator name asserts the STEM subset of tertiary enrollment expressed as a gross ratio. The best available evidence measures TOTAL tertiary gross enrollment across all fields of study: the World Bank/UIS SE.TER.ENRR page lists 'Egypt, Arab Rep. 2025 38' and the UNESCO IESALC Higher Education Policy Observatory country profile lists 'GER, both sexes (%): 38.0% (In 2024...)'. Neither disaggregates by field of study. The nearest field-related Egyptian evidence, CAPMAS's annual higher-education bulletin press release, reports headcounts split into 'theoretical' and 'practical' faculties (e.g. private universities: 125 theoretical colleges with 72.1 thousand students, 19.8%, and 323 practical colleges with 292.9 thousand students, 80.2%), but 'practical' is not the ISCED STEM aggregate (it includes medicine, pharmacy, nursing, applied arts) and headcount shares are not a gross enrollment ratio against the 5-year post-secondary age cohort. Deriving a STEM GER from these parts would be a construction, not a published figure. An independent T1 series (UNESCO Institute for Statistics — percentage of graduates from STEM programmes in tertiary education (FOSGP.5T8.F500600700)) reports 14.05 for 2025.

4.6.value: Egypt has a published National Artificial Intelligence Strategy (developed by the Cabinet-established National Council for Artificial Intelligence under presidential mandate, published by MCIT in July 2021, with a Second
4.6.src: Arab Republic of Egypt, National Council for Artificial Intelligence / MCIT — Egypt National Artificial Intelligence Strategy
4.6.note: Quoted text is the strategy's own table of contents; the retrieved extract does not include the body text of the agriculture section. Next level not proposed: Operating was not claimed because none of the retrieved pages document delivered implementation of the agriculture component — no implementation report, budget execution, or deployed agricultural AI service is evidenced in the supplied text (the OECD review page supplies only an abstract and front matter, not findings). Level 4 was not proposed because quality_evidence is empty: the only independent source retrieved (OECD Artificial Intelligence Review of Egypt, T2) is present here as an abstract that speaks to implementation of the OECD AI Principles rather than to the performance of the strategy or its agriculture pillar, and the OECD.AI navigator entry for the 2025-2030 strategy records 'Has this initiative been evaluated? No'. Level 5 was not proposed because scale_evidence is empty: the only figures available (7.7% ICT GDP contribution, 30,000 AI experts, 250+ startups, 36% population using AI tools) are 2030 targets, i.e. stated ambition, not published reach. The named construct is a national AI strategy containing an agriculture component. The quoted government artifact is the national AI strategy itself and its table of contents lists a dedicated sub-section on Agriculture, Water Management and Environment within the 'AI for Development' pillar, so both halves of the construct are met. On the census's open question (publication vs. formal executive approval): both tests are satisfied here — the document carries a statement by the President of the Republic mandating it, and the Executive Summary records that 'In November 2019, the Egyptian Cabinet approved the formation of the National Council for Artificial Intelligence (NCAI)' whose 'main objective is to formalize and govern the implementation of Egypt's National AI Strategy'; it is also officially published on the government AI portal and by MCIT. The evidence therefore does not sit on the contested side of that question.
4.6.tier_detail: Quoted text is the strategy's own table of contents; the retrieved extract does not include the body text of the agriculture section.

5.4.value: DATA GAP — 1) CAPMAS main data portal (capmas.gov.eg/data) — navigation shell only, no indicator values. 2) CAPMAS microdata catalog entry for the 2022/23 Economic Census — questionnaires include an agriculture form but no digital-literacy statistic is published on the page. 3) IFPRI/CGIAR policy note 'Digital Literacy Training to Promote Diffusion of Digital Agricultural Tools to Smallholder Farmers' (Sept 2024) — contains the baseline barrier figures (54/52/49/19/16/14 percent) for Minya and Benisuef; inverse-direction, sub-national. 4) IFPRI Discussion Paper 02359 (Sept 2025), the full version — reports treatment effects (uptake +20 pp, utilization +26 pp, trust +8-13 pp) but no baseline digital-literacy prevalence rate for Egyptian farmers. 5) MCIT news page on Digital Decent Life rural digital-skills training — programme description and a 2,000-trainee target, no rate. 6) OUCI abstract record of Mansour (2023), Library Hi Tech, ICT use among 131 farmers in Qena — qualitative/descriptive findings on ICT use and illiteracy as an obstacle, no digital-literacy percentage. 7) Arabic news item relaying a CAPMAS Literacy Day release — conventional literacy rates (16.6 percent national, 20.3 percent rural, 2024), wrong construct and T5 publisher. Dead ends: no ITU, Findex or World Bank farmer-disaggregated digital-skills figure for Egypt appeared in the retrieved set.
5.4.note: Nearest available evidence is a purposive, project-recruited sample in two governorates; measure is self-reported perceived barrier, not an assessed skills test. Next level not proposed: The evidence does not establish any nationally representative measurement of farmer digital literacy in Egypt — no CAPMAS survey module, no ITU/Findex farmer-disaggregated skills figure, and no government publication of such a rate was found in the retrieved pages; therefore even level 1 cannot be evidenced as a measured value rather than an inference. The indicator names a percentage of farmers who ARE digitally literate, at national scope. The available Egyptian evidence (IFPRI policy note, RCT baseline in Minya and Benisuef) reports that about half of sampled farmers — 52 percent — cited 'general digital literacy' / 'farmer digital illiteracy' as a key challenge to using mobile applications, alongside 54 percent citing unawareness of apps and 49 percent lacking smartphone access; roughly 2,400 of 4,000 farmers in the sample owned smartphones. These are (a) inverse-direction, (b) self-reported barrier perceptions rather than measured skills, and (c) two-governorate, project-beneficiary samples, not national. CAPMAS pages retrieved carry no farmer digital-literacy statistic; the only CAPMAS-derived figures surfaced concern conventional (reading/writing) illiteracy — 16.6 percent nationally and 20.3 percent rural in 2024 — a different construct again, and surfaced only via a T5 news site. MCIT's Digital Decent Life page describes rural digital-skills training activity (target of 2,000 students) but publishes no literacy rate. WHERE THIS LIVES: Demographic and Health Survey 2014 - IPUMS Subset (2014-2014) collects internet and device access among farming households in 4 variable(s), including W_SMARTPHONE, B_SMARTPHONE, C_SMARTPHONE. https://microdata.worldbank.org/catalog/3093 That survey is too old to carry a current-state claim on its own. No value is taken from it here.

5.5.value: For Egypt, admissible evidence establishes only an announced/intended digital extension agenda: an IFPRI policy note (2020) records that digitalizing agricultural extension is a recommended policy direction resting on 'o
5.5.src: IFPRI (CGSpace) — Symposium policy note 2: Digitalization of agricultural services and policy analysis in Egypt, MENA Policy Note 12
5.5.note: Policy-note synthesis of seminar findings and recommendations, not an inventory or evaluation of deployed extension services. Next level not proposed: Adopted was not proposed because no admissible T1-T3 document retrieved records a formally adopted national digital extension instrument — no decree, ministerial programme document, budget line or service charter for a named platform appears in the supplied pages. The only account of a concrete platform (GeoAgro-Misr) and of an institutional framework (Agriculture Digital Extension Network, ADEN) sits on a T5 aggregator abstract page (exa.ai), which is below the T1-T3 bar this prerequisite row requires; the underlying CGIAR full text (Source 5) resolved to a login screen and could not be quoted. Operating was likewise not reachable: no published user counts, governorate coverage, advisory volumes or evaluations of any Egyptian digital extension service appear in any admissible source, so neither quality_evidence nor scale_evidence could be filled. The IFPRI note is squarely about digitalization of agricultural extension in Egypt, so it addresses the named construct; however it characterises the state of play in terms of recommendations and 'ongoing projects' rather than documenting a named, adopted national digital extension instrument with defined operations.
5.5.tier_detail: Policy-note synthesis of seminar findings and recommendations, not an inventory or evaluation of deployed extension services

5.7.value: A Digital Transformation Unit (AG-DTU) was formally established inside Egypt's Ministry of Agriculture and Land Reclamation under MCIT ministerial decree no. 605 of 15 March 2020, with an initial complement of 16 experts
5.7.src: MALR / IFPRI-EU planning workshop presentation, 'Building the Digital Transformation Unit of the Ministry of Agriculture and Land Reclamation' (Dr. Mohamed El Kersh, MALR), hosted on CGSpace
5.7.note: Slide deck presented by a MALR official at a donor-funded planning workshop; describes the unit's establishment and forward plan rather than an independent verification of its operation. Most recent confirmation of the unit dates from February 2021. Next level not proposed: Operating was not asserted, and in any case would not raise the level: the only document describing the unit is a February 2021 planning-workshop deck written in prospective terms ('DTU will be directly under the supervision of the Minister', 'seeking additional resources... to support the establishment of the unit'), and no later official source retrieved — including MALR's own site and the OECD AI Review of Egypt — confirms the unit is functioning, names it, or reports its outputs. Level 4 was not proposed because quality_evidence is empty: there is no evaluation, audit, performance report or service standard for the unit; the only account of it is the implementer's own presentation, which is design, not quality. Level 5 was not proposed because scale_evidence is empty: no reach figures exist for the unit (the 16-expert headcount is an input, not coverage or beneficiaries, and the ministry-wide digital service figures quoted elsewhere — 3.5 million farmer cards printed, 20 e-services piloted — belong to the joint MALR-MCIT programme, not to this unit). The indicator name asserts a standing 'digital/AI' unit inside the ministry of agriculture. The confirmed instrument is a Digital Transformation Unit (AG-DTU) established by MCIT decree 605 of 15 March 2020 within MALR — a digital unit, and therefore on the right side of the construct for the 'digital' half. It is not an AI unit: its named components are Workflow and Government Services, GIS, and AG-FORESIGHT (foresight/policy modeling with EU-IFPRI support). The AI-labelled activity in Egyptian agriculture (the Hudhud AI advisory app, AI-based crop-area estimation) is documented on MALR's own site as a joint MALR-MCIT programme (Source 5), not as the output of a named AI unit inside MALR. The AI institutional home in Egypt sits at MCIT (National Council for AI, Applied Innovation Center — Source 7 navigation), not in the agriculture ministry. Nothing on MALR's own current websites (Sources 4 and 6, including the organisational-structure menus) names a digital or AI unit.
5.7.tier_detail: Slide deck presented by a MALR official at a donor-funded planning workshop; describes the unit's establishment and forward plan rather than an independent verification of its operation. Most recent confirmation of the unit dates from February 2021.

5.12.value: DATA GAP — Started with CAPMAS agriculture and water resources subject page (capmas.gov.eg/data/mainSubject/1/subSubject/16): navigation shell only, no tables in retrieved text. Went to CAPMAS censusinfo metadata for the 2011 Basic ICT Indicators survey of internet companies (catalog/75 datafile F15 and variable V397): confirmed sex-disaggregated ICT-staff variables exist, but the universe is internet service companies (categories A&B), not agriculture, the year is 2011, and V397 gives raw counts (mean 41.2, max 204, 6 records) rather than a share. Checked CAPMAS Labor Force Survey 2022 metadata overview (catalog/1842): objectives confirm sex, occupation and economic-activity disaggregation are collected, but the page publishes no tabulated result, and no ICT-occupation-within-agriculture cross-tab appears. Tried the CGIAR GENDER platform item on social equity, women and youth in the digital transformation of Egyptian agriculture the most on-construct candidate but the page returned 'Error: access denied' and yielded no text to quote. Reviewed AUC Social Research Center working paper 'Impact of ICT on Gender Gap in Egypt' (2009): retrieved text is front matter and preface, giving female economic participation around 20% economy-wide, nothing on agriculture-ICT roles. Reviewed the MPED round-table release: richest set of gender figures but all about agricultural labor, land ownership and internet use. Reviewed the Fund for Youth Employment MENA digital-jobs report: Egypt chapter is qualitative on barriers, no workforce-share statistic in the retrieved text, and the domain tiers as T5 which bars statistical use anyway. Dead end on all routes; no page supplies a digital-agriculture workforce gender share for Egypt.
5.12.note: Next level not proposed: The evidence does not show any count or share of women among agricultural extension officers, agtech firm employees, or ICT-in-agriculture staff in Egypt. Until CAPMAS or the Ministry of Agriculture publishes a sex-disaggregated headcount for such roles or the assessment ratifies which population counts no rung, including level 1, can be evidenced. Closest quantified evidence, all on the wrong side of the construct: (1) Egypt's Ministry of Planning and Economic Development (T3, 27 Nov 2021 round table release) reports that the agricultural sector employs 45% of women in the labor force versus 24% of men, that 94% of harvesting in Upper Egypt and 67% in Lower Egypt is done by women, that less than 5% of land is owned by women, and that women's internet use is 47% versus 69% for men. These describe women's share of agricultural labor and the general gender digital divide years earlier than the 45% figure and is aggregate ICT, not agriculture. (3) CAPMAS Labor Force Survey 2022 metadata lists sex, occupation and economic activity as survey dimensions but the retrieved overview page carries no tabulated values, and an occupation-by-activity cross-tab identifying ICT roles inside agriculture is not published there. (4) The Fund for Youth Employment MENA report (T5 domain) covers women in digital jobs in Egypt qualitatively with no digital-ag workforce share. Adopting the 45% agricultural-employment figure would place this row at level 3 on a statistic that measures female participation in farm labor, not in the digital-agriculture workforce. WHERE THIS LIVES: Enterprise Survey 2008 (2008-2008) collects sex composition of the workforce in 1 variable(s), including q107d. https://microdata.worldbank.org/catalog/158 That survey is too old to carry a current-state claim on its own. No value is taken from it here.

5.8.value: Egypt operates a national data-science/AI training pipeline — the Ministry of Communications and Information Technology's Digital Egypt Pioneers Initiative (DEPI), launched in 2023, whose seven tracks include "AI and Dat
5.8.src: Ministry of Communications and Information Technology (Egypt), Human Development — MCIT — Digital Egypt Pioneers Initiative
5.8.note: RATIFICATION HOLD — The indicator name has two halves and the retrieved evidence sits entirely on the data-science side. DEPI is a sector-generic national ICT/AI talent programme: its listed tracks are AI and Data Science, Infrastructure and Cybersecurity, Management and ERP, Digital Marketing and Arts, Software Development, Data Analytics, Digital Game Creation, and its DEPI Industry tracks cover education, legal, finance, software, marketing and healthcare applications — agriculture appears in none of them. On the other side, Egyptian agricultural training exists but carries no data-science content in the sources retrieved: CAPMAS reports 256 agricultural technical secondary schools with 225.5 thousand students and 59.1 thousand agricultural high-school graduates in 2018/2019, and the technical-institute bulletin records the agriculture group at 1.7% of technical institute graduates. The only agriculture-plus-digital training retrieved is IFPRI's randomised digital-literacy training for smallholder farmers in Egypt, which is farmer end-user training, not a professional agtech/data-science training pipeline. So if the slash is conjunctive (a pipeline producing agtech data-science skills), the named instrument is absent; if disjunctive, the data-science half is operating at national scale. This cell is recorded on the disjunctive reading and should be re-scored to Absent if the definition is ratified as conjunctive.. The level is withheld and this row leaves every mean. Implementer's own programme description; no third-party verification of the training pipeline in the retrieved pages.

6.3.value: DATA GAP — 1) B-READY 'Geographical coverage' page — read the full B-READY 2024 list of 50 economies; MENA entries are Iraq, Morocco, West Bank and Gaza; Egypt absent. The 2025 list (52 additional economies) is truncated in the retrieved text at 'Mali', so Egypt could not be confirmed or excluded there from this page. 2) B-READY main landing page and Publications page — describe the 2025 interim report covering 101 economies and its three headline messages, but carry no country-level scores. 3) Data360 Business Ready dataset record — '3 Indicators | 2024 | 50 Economies', consistent with Egypt being outside the 2024 sample. 4) B-READY 2024 full report PDF (documents1.worldbank.org) and the openknowledge mirror — only front matter and table of contents were retrieved; Appendix A (Topic Scores) content was not in the supplied text, and in any case Egypt is not in the 2024 sample. 5) Business Ready 2025 documents-and-reports record — abstract only, no country tables. 6) World Bank Data Blog on B-READY in WDI — explains the 0-100 pillar/topic scoring and names top performers, no Egypt figure. 7) GAFI (investinegypt.gov.eg, 23-07-2025) — Egypt-specific, but reports that Egypt is 'intensifying its preparations for participation in the Business Ready 2026 (B-READY 2026) report', i.e. an announced future participation, not a published score. The B-READY 2025 interim edition covers 101 economies, but the coverage table for 2025 in the retrieved page is truncated mid-list (ends at 'Mali'), so Egypt's inclusion could not be verified from the supplied text; the Egyptian government's own investment authority (GAFI, July 2025) describes Egypt as preparing to participate in B-READY 2026, which is consistent with Egypt not yet having a published B-READY score. 6.9.value: Across the retrieved evidence base for Egypt — a 2025 IFPRI/CGIAR policy note on Egypt's digital agriculture ecosystem, MCIT's ICT indicator bulletin, GAFI's investment portal, CAPMAS agricultural statistics, and Egypt's

8.2.src: World Bank Open Data — Account ownership at a financial institution or with a mobile-money-service provider, female (% of population ages 15+), Egypt, Arab Rep. (Global Findex Database)

Next level not proposed: Level 4 would require female account ownership above 60%. The published Findex/WDI figure for Egypt is 40.21%, only marginally above the 40 cut, and no T1 demand-side source in the retrieved pages puts Egyptian female account ownership above 60%. The CBE's 72.5% women's figure is a supply-side administrative measure of active accounts (bank, postal, wallet, prepaid card) as of June 2026, not the survey-based account-ownership construct, and is not admissible as the value for this cell. The quoted series is WDI/Global Findex FX.OWN.TOTL.FE.ZS, female account ownership at a financial institution OR with a mobile-money-service provider, ages 15+ — i.e. exactly the sex-disaggregated 'account ownership, female' the indicator names. On the unratified definitional question: this series folds mobile-money accounts into the total, so it overlaps with the construct scored separately at 8.4, and the Egypt figure is therefore partly driven by mobile-wallet uptake rather than bank accounts alone; a bank-account-only female figure is not published in the retrieved pages. Context on the wrong side of the definition question: the Central Bank of Egypt (T3, supply-side Financial Inclusion Datahub, counting bank accounts, postal accounts, mobile wallets and prepaid cards) reports a far higher women's rate — 'women’s financial inclusion rate rose substantially from 19.1% in 2016 to 72.5% by the end of June 2026' — a different, administrative-register construct with a different reference date, not used as the value here. Corroborated by an independent T1 series (World Bank WDI FX.OWN.TOTL.FE.ZS (Global Findex wave)): 40.21 for 2024.

8.6.value: DATA GAP — 1) Checked the two GSMA Mobile Gender Gap Reports (2023, 2024) supplied — these are the canonical source for this construct, but the retrieved text covers only front matter, contents and LMIC-level aggregates; Egypt is not shown among the 12 surveyed countries in the retrieved text, and no Egypt figure appears anywhere in the supplied text. Also noted the construct mismatch (relative gap on male base vs pp). 2) Checked CAPMAS microdata catalog pages: HIECS 2015 overview (household-level possession of communication means, no sex disaggregation, no figures); Egypt Family Health Survey 2021 women's data dictionary (contains Q121 mobile use and Q122 'Do you own Mobile phone' for women only — a promising source for a female ownership rate, but the page lists variables with no tabulated results and there is no male counterpart on the page); BEIMIS 2011 variable page (household barrier variable 'وجود هاتف محمول يفى بالغرض', unweighted record counts only, not sex-disaggregated ownership); 2013/14 telecom bulletin related-materials page (no data in text); 2016/17 Annual Telecommunications Bulletin (subscription/exchange statistics, no individual ownership by sex). 3) Checked MCIT 'ICT Indicators in Brief' January 2020 — mobile penetration 95.34% and subscription figures, all national and subscription-based, no sex disaggregation. 4) Checked the Pertanika article on ICT and women's empowerment in Egypt — states the gender divide in mobile ownership exists and cites MCIT data for 2009/2010, but the values are in chart images not present in the retrieved text, and the supplied domain tier is T5. Dead ends: no ITU, Findex or World Bank gender-disaggregated ownership page for Egypt was supplied. Conclusion: figure not present in the supplied pages; recording a hold rather than constructing a value.
8.6.note: Next level not proposed: Not applicable in the usual sense because no level is proposed; the specific missing element is any Egypt-specific numeric male and female phone-ownership rate, or a stated pp gap, in an admissible-tier page among those supplied. The indicator name fixes the unit as percentage points (presumably male ownership rate minus female ownership rate, in pp). The closest widely quoted measure for the same construct, GSMA's mobile gender gap, is a RELATIVE gap computed on a male-ownership base ((male% - female%)/male%), which is a different number and would be inadmissible as a pp value even if an Egypt figure had appeared; the supplied GSMA 2023 and 2024 report texts contain only LMIC aggregates (e.g. '83% of women now own a mobile phone' across LMICs in 2023) and no Egypt row. The CAPMAS Egypt Family Health Survey 2021 data dictionary shows the underlying question exists for women ('Q122 Do you own Mobile phone'), i.e. Egypt collects sex-specific ownership data, but the supplied page is a variable list with no tabulated ownership rate for either sex, so no gap can be quoted. The Pertanika article states males' mobile phone ownership is 'much higher compared to females' for 2009 and 2010 but reports it only in an embedded chart (Fig.1) with no numeric values in the retrieved text, and the domain tier supplied is T5, which cannot carry a statistic.

This is corroborated on the same page by the account-ownership-by-type breakdown ('8%' mobile money account only plus '8%' bank and mobile money account = 16%). The figure is national (all adults 15+), not rural-specific and not agriculture-specific; the indicator as named ('Mobile money account (%)') does not restrict to a subpopulation, so the construct matches. Context not used as the value: the Central Bank of Egypt reports an overall financial inclusion rate of 77.6% at end-2025, but that counts bank accounts, Egypt Post accounts, mobile wallets and prepaid cards together and is therefore a different construct.
