8.9.value: DATA GAP — 1. Checked the two CAPMAS NADA catalog pages (Agriculture collection, 47 studies; Central Data Catalog, 629 studies) for any bulletin or survey on farmer ICT/digital service use — the agriculture holdings are income estimates, production movement, animal disease, cooperative activity and property/rent bulletins; nothing on digital service reach. Opened the two individual CAPMAS study pages retrieved (Agricultural Income Estimates 2015-2016; Cooperative Activity 2018/2019) and the Arabic Economic Census 2022/2023 record — the census questionnaires include an agriculture form and a telecommunications form but the retrieved page lists only file names, no smallholder digital-reach figure. 2. Read the IFPRI policy note (Sept 2024) and IFPRI Discussion Paper 02359 (Sept 2025) in full text as supplied: these are the substantive Egypt evidence, but the population is ~4,000 smallholders in Minya and Beni Suef within GIZ AIP farmer organizations; figures reported are baseline barrier shares and treatment effects, not national coverage. 3. Read the GIZ AIP baseline assessment (T4) table of contents as supplied — outputs concern farmer organization customer structure, management capacity and productivity innovations; no digital-reach percentage appears in the retrieved text. 4. Read the RESILINK/InovFarmer.MED deck (T5): Tawa village, Beni Suef, N=128, 13.28% use of mobile applications in agriculture — sub-national, T5, and a narrower construct. 5. Dead end: the Heliyon PMC article surfaced by search is about smallholder adoption of digital agricultural services in the Bono East Region of GHANA, plus a CTA continental figure of 33 million African smallholders reached — evidence about other countries and a continental aggregate, explicitly not usable for Egypt. Conclusion: no Egypt-national smallholder digital-reach figure exists in the supplied pages.
8.9.note: Next level not proposed: Not applicable in the usual form because no level is proposed; the specific missing thing is any nationally representative measurement of Egyptian smallholders reached by digital services, and any published definition of 'reached' (registered, active, or benefiting) against which such a measurement could be taken. Even level 1 (below 10) cannot be asserted, because no source rules out that national reach exceeds 10% — the two-governorate baseline shows 2,400 of 4,000 sampled farmers already own smartphones and the RCT's post-training uptake gains are in the 20-26 percentage point range. The indicator names a NATIONAL share of SMALLHOLDERS reached by digital services. The best available evidence sits on the wrong side of that question in two ways. (1) Scope: IFPRI Discussion Paper 02359 / Policy Note (Sept 2024, Sept 2025) reports on a purposively selected population of about 4,000 smallholders in Minya and Beni Suef who are members of ~30 GIZ Agricultural Innovation Project farmer organizations — an intervention sample, not a national frame; within it 2,400 of the 4,000 own smartphones and the trial targeted only those. Its impact estimates (standard digital training raised uptake by 20 percentage points and utilization by 26 percentage points) are treatment effects, not coverage rates. Baseline barrier shares (54% unaware of existing digital applications, 52% citing digital illiteracy, 49% lacking smartphone access) describe constraints, not reach. (2) Scope and construct: the RESILINK/InovFarmer.MED slide deck reports that in Tawa village, Beni Suef (N=128, ~10% of village holders), 46.12% had knowledge of ICT/IoT concepts, 18.8% had ICT training, and only 13.28% used mobile applications in agriculture — a single-village sample, and 'use of mobile applications in agriculture' is a narrower construct than 'reached by digital services'. Recording either as a national smallholder reach percentage would convert a data gap into a confident figure.

8.11.value: DATA GAP — Order of examination: (1) CAPMAS censusinfo household e-indicators 2011 data dictionary — scanned all 229 listed variables for a language field; only 'عدم المعرفة باللغة الإنجليزية' (lack of English knowledge as a barrier to computer use) appears, which is a barrier variable, not a service-language share. (2) CAPMAS ISP survey questionnaire (form A-B) — service-type and coverage questions only, no language-of-service item. (3) CAPMAS ISP variable V45 — the one explicitly language-tagged variable found, 'number of client websites hosted in Arabic'; rejected as a different construct (hosting count, no denominator, commercial web, 2011). (4) CAPMAS Egypt Statistics Journal (Aug 2017) — census/population content, nothing on service languages. (5) OECD e-Government Studies: Egypt 2013 — retrieved text is foreword/acknowledgements; no language-availability statistic surfaced in the supplied extract. (6) Cairo University ICT diffusion paper — macroeconomic and diffusion indicators only; literacy is discussed as a correlate, not service language. (7) MCIT press release on 2025 ICT achievements and the Arabic Digital Egypt strategy page — rich on service counts, users and request volumes, silent on language of delivery. (8) 6Wresearch Egypt Language Services Market — T5 vendor material, narrative only, and inadmissible for a statistic under the tier rules. Dead end throughout: no publisher in the supplied set reports a local-language service share for Egypt.
8.11.note: Next level not proposed: Not applicable — no level proposed. For any level to be defensible the evidence would need (a) a defined universe of digital agricultural or government services for Egypt, and (b) a count or share of those services available in Arabic or other local languages. Neither exists in the supplied pages; even the highest-quality T1 item (CAPMAS) gives an unnormalised count of Arabic-language hosted websites with no denominator. Indicator names a PERCENTAGE of services available in local languages. The only language-tagged statistic in the supplied pages is CAPMAS's 2011 ISP survey variable 'عدد المواقع المستضافة لصالح العملاء باللغــة العربيـة' (number of client websites hosted in Arabic) — an absolute count of hosted websites from six responding ISPs, not a share of services, not agricultural, and 14+ years old. Contextual figures that are NOT answers to this cell: MCIT reports 210 government services on the Digital Egypt platform in 2025 (up from 170 in 2024) with 10.7 million users, but publishes no language breakdown; the MCIT Digital Egypt strategy page is itself written in Arabic, which is suggestive but is not a published measurement. This cell sits squarely on the wrong side of the unratified definitional question: no Egyptian publisher supplies a denominator for local-language service delivery, so a %-share formulation is currently unmeasurable for Egypt from official sources.

A1-CAND-IMP.value: DATA GAP — 1) Checked UNdata/FAOSTAT 'Cereal import dependency ratio (percent) (3-year average)' (Source 2), the canonical T1 source for this exact indicator \u2014 Egypt is listed as a selectable country but the rendered page text stops at Albania (page 1 of 81 records); no Egypt value present to quote. 2) Checked FAO openknowledge Figure 52 'Cereal import dependency ratio, top countries (2017\u20132019)' (Source 6) \u2014 lists only ~20 top-ranked countries; Egypt not among them. 3) Checked FAO GIEWS Country Brief Egypt (Sources 1 and 3) \u2014 gives cereal import requirements in tonnes and production forecasts, no dependency ratio. 4) Checked USDA FAS Grain and Feed Annual Egypt (Source 8) \u2014 wheat/corn production, consumption and import tonnages only, no ratio. 5) Checked UN Comtrade cereals for Egypt (Source 5) \u2014 trade values/weights only. 6) Checked Springer Food Security Egypt/Jordan paper (Source 7) \u2014 states 50% food import dependence for Egypt, a different construct. 7) Checked CAPMAS metadata catalog entry (Source 4) \u2014 bibliographic record only, no figures. 8) Food Systems Dashboard page (Source 10) blocked by a browser verification checkpoint, no data returned. Conclusion: the figure very likely exists in FAOSTAT's Suite of Food Security Indicators for Egypt, but it is not in the supplied pages, so nothing is recorded.
A1-CAND-IMP.note: Next level not proposed: No level proposed because this is an unscored carried candidate and, separately, no admissible Egypt-specific value for the named construct was quotable from the supplied pages. Nearest available Egypt-specific figures in the retrieved pages measure different constructs: (a) Springer/Food Security (Source 7) states Egypt and Jordan are 'highly dependent on food imports (Egypt 50%, Jordan 95%)' \u2014 this is overall food import dependence, not the FAO cereal import dependency ratio (cereal imports / (production + imports \u2212 exports)); (b) FAO GIEWS (Sources 1 and 3) gives Egypt's 2026/27 cereal import requirement in tonnes (29 million tonnes, of which wheat 13.5 million and maize 15.5 million) \u2014 a volume, not a ratio; (c) UN Comtrade (Source 5) gives cereal trade values and weights, not a dependency ratio. Converting any of these into a percentage would be a derived estimate, not a published figure.

8.17.value: DATA GAP — 1) CAPMAS microdata catalog (T1) — central catalog and Agriculture collection pages listed: 47 agriculture studies covering income estimates, prices, animal disease, cooperative activity; no climate-advisory or extension-reach variable surfaced. The one variable-level page retrieved (V3121, 2011 social services bulletin) codes types of agricultural services delivered by local units, not advisory receipt. 2) FAO STI Portal (T1) entry for Egypt's Early Climate Warning app — confirms existence, maturity and target group (Upper Egypt farmers) but its own text states specific adoption rates are not provided. 3) IFAD SAIL supervision report (T1) — lists Early Warning System and CCICRE among acronyms and rates 'Adaptation to Climate Change' 4/6, but the retrieved text carries no advisory-reach figure. 4) WFP Egypt publication page (T1) — gives Upper Egypt livelihood shares (63% of zone employment, ~85% of rural households) but nothing on advisory reach. 5) IFPRI/CGIAR CSA policy seminar note (T2) — richest description of the advisory supply chain (EMA forecasts, CCIC daily warnings, Bashaer, Nabta, FAO regional EWS review) and explicitly flags a communication gap, unquantified. 6) Scientific Reports farmer survey, seven governorates (T2) — measures awareness/adaptation, not advisory receipt. 7) FAO geodata toolkit link returned a 404 page. 8) Sada Elbalad (T5) — expansion of extension and digital advisory services, 7,000+ wheat demonstration fields; existence facts only, ineligible for a statistic. 8.17.note: Next level not proposed: Not applicable — no level proposed. The specific missing element is any published numerator/denominator or survey-based share of Egyptian farmers receiving climate or agro-meteorological advisories; the strongest retrieved statement on receipt is qualitative and negative (smallholders often never receive warnings), with no figure attached. The indicator name — 'Climate advisory reach (%)' — reads as farmer-side receipt: the share of farmers/farm households actually reached by climate advisories. Every retrieved Egyptian source sits on the supply side of the census's open question. The IFPRI/CGIAR policy note (T2) describes the Climate Change Information Center issuing daily climate warnings and the Bashaer platform delivering tailored climate-smart recommendations, and explicitly records the opposite of a reach figure — that communication gaps mean many smallholders never receive the warnings — but attaches no percentage to either issuance or receipt. The Scientific Reports study of 2,953 farmers across seven governorates (T2) reports high climate awareness alongside rare adoption of digital tools, but its abstract as retrieved gives no percentage for advisory receipt, and awareness is in any case a different construct from advisory reach. The news item (T5) cites more than 7,000 wheat demonstration fields — an activity count, not a reach share, and T5 material cannot carry a statistic. CAPMAS catalog pages retrieved contain no climate-advisory variable at all.

The indicator's name fixes the outcome as YIELD or INCOME attributable to digital agriculture. The only retrieved Egypt evidence with hard yield/income outcomes is a peer-reviewed Applied Water Science field study (Springer, 2025) on replacing flood irrigation of sugarcane with drip irrigation in Upper Egypt, which reports water-use efficiency +44%, sugarcane yield +22% and net profit +50%. Conversely, the World Bank 2021 report and the CGSpace e-extension paper are on the right treatment (digital technologies / e-extension) but the retrieved text yields no realised yield or income outcome — consistent with the indicator census note that Egypt's existing level 3 rests on an evaluation measuring diffusion and adoption rather than yield or income. 1.3.name: Employment in agriculture (%)

answer.source_title: World Bank, World Development Indicators — Employment in agriculture (% of total employment) (modeled ILO estimate), Egypt, Arab Rep.
answer.quote: Egypt, Arab Rep.	2025	18
answer.data_quality_flag: ILO modelled estimate (ILOEST) nowcast for 2025, not a directly observed survey figure; World Bank portal displays the value rounded to whole percent
answer.construct_note: The indicator name 'Employment in agriculture (%)' omits its denominator; the quoted series is explicitly '% of total employment', which is the standard reading. The series also covers ISIC-A (agriculture, hunting, forestry and fishing), i.e. slightly broader than agriculture alone — this is the open definitional question flagged in the indicator census. The reference-year 2025 figure is an ILO MODELLED nowcast rather than an observed labour force survey result. An observed national figure sits alongside it: CAPMAS's 2024 annual labour force survey, as reported by the State Information Service (T3), states 'Agriculture and fishing remained the largest employment sectors, engaging 5.594 million workers, representing 18.7 percent of the workforce' — consistent with the modelled 18 and confirming the modelled series is not drifting from national data. A commercial T5 aggregator (statbase.org) reproduces the same ILOSTAT series at 17.52 percent for 2025 and 17.98 for 2024, i.e. the unrounded value behind the World Bank's 18.
answer.quality_evidence: Primary value is from the World Bank WDI portal (T1) sourcing the ILO Modelled Estimates database (ILOEST), accessed January 2026, licensed CC BY-4.0. Cross-checked against an independent, survey-based national source: CAPMAS Annual Labour Force Survey 2024 reported by the Egyptian State Information Service, giving 18.7 percent of the workforce in agriculture and fishing (5.594 million of 29.928 million employed). The two agree to within one percentage point, so the modelled nowcast is not carrying the cell alone.
answer.scale_evidence: National coverage, all employed persons aged 15+. CAPMAS reports total employment of 29.928 million in 2024, of which 5.594 million in agriculture and fishing.
answer.rung_argument: The value itself, not an aggregation, drives the score, so the argument is about whether 18 is the right number for the named construct. (1) A figure exists for Egypt specifically: World Bank/ILOEST publishes 18 for reference year 2025. (2) It is on the correct denominator — the series is titled '% of total employment', which is what the indicator name implicitly requires. (3) It is not an artefact of modelling: the independent CAPMAS 2024 labour force survey puts agriculture and fishing at 18.7 percent of the workforce, so the observed and modelled figures corroborate each other. (4) Against the cut points (lower is better: above 45 = 1, 30-45 = 2, 15-30 = 3, 5-15 = 4, below 5 = 5), 18 clears the 45 and 30 cuts and therefore sits at level 3.
answer.negative_finding: Level 4 would require the agricultural employment share to have fallen below 15 percent of total employment. It has not: the ILO modelled 2025 value is 18 (17.52 unrounded on the same ILOSTAT series per the T5 aggregator), and the observed CAPMAS 2024 survey figure is higher still at 18.7 percent. Neither the modelled nor the survey-based measure is within three points of the 15 cut, and the series is declining by roughly half a point per year, so no published figure supports the next rung.
answer.search_trail: Started with the World Bank WDI country page for SL.AGR.EMPL.ZS filtered to Egypt (T1) — carries Egypt 2025 = 18 in both the 'Selected Countries' and 'All Countries' tables, sourced to ILOEST. Found the sectoral breakdown instead in the State Information Service report of the CAPMAS 2024 annual LFS (T3): 18.7 percent in agriculture and fishing — used as corroboration in construct_note rather than as the recorded value, since the World Bank T1 series is the register's series. Reviewed FAOSTAT Analytical Briefs 92 and 110 (openknowledge.fao.org, T2) — both give only global and regional shares (26.1 percent globally in 2023; Africa 46 percent) with no Egypt country row in the retrieved text, so they are not evidence for this country. statbase.org (T5) reproduces the ILOSTAT series with unrounded values (17.52 for 2025) but is vendor material and cannot carry a statistic, so it is cited only as context on rounding.

The published series actually retrieved is WDI NV.AGR.EMPL.KD, whose long definition covers 'Agriculture, forestry, and fishing ... ISIC (Rev. 4) divisions 01-03' and is denominated in constant 2015 US$, not current USD. So the evidence sits on the broader-scope, constant-price side of the unratified definitional question: sector scope is wider than 'agriculture' alone (it includes forestry and fishing), and the price basis is a 2015 constant-dollar series rather than the bare 'USD' the name implies. The current-US$ counterpart (NV.AGR.TOTL.CD divided by employment) is not published as a per-worker series in these pages, so no alternative figure on the narrower reading exists here. Figure is national for Egypt, which is what the indicator asks for.
answer.quality_evidence: T1 publisher (World Bank WDI, jointly with ILOSTAT), CC BY-4.0, with full metadata glossary retrieved (Sources 2 and 3) documenting definition, aggregation method and known limitations. The figure is read directly from the country table on the indicator's own World Bank data page, not from a secondary re-publication. A French-language mirror of the same World Bank page (Source 10) carries the identical Egypt value of 8 942,42 for 2025, corroborating the read.
answer.scale_evidence: National coverage for Egypt, Arab Rep.; annual series 1991-2025; most recent year 2025.
answer.rung_argument: The route taken is the single-published-figure route, so the argument is about the value and its construct match rather than arithmetic. (a) A named, quotable figure exists for Egypt specifically: 8,942.42 for reference year 2025, on the World Bank's own indicator page. (b) The figure is the labour-productivity ratio the indicator names — sector value added divided by sector employment — per the metadata: 'Value added per worker is calculated by dividing value added of a sector by the number employed in the sector.' (c) It is expressed in US dollars, satisfying the '(USD)' in the name, albeit constant 2015 US$. (d) It is national and current (2025), not a stale or sub-national proxy. Applying the cut points: 8942.42 clears 1000, 2500 and 5000, placing Egypt at level 4.
answer.negative_finding: Level 5 was not proposed because the published value, 8,942.42 constant 2015 US$, falls short of the 10000 cut point by roughly 1,058 dollars. No source in the retrieved pages publishes an Egypt figure at or above 10000 for this construct on any price basis or any reference year; the Arab World aggregate does exceed 10000 (10,945.1 in 2025) but that is a regional aggregate, not Egypt, and cannot be substituted. Should the definition be ratified as current US$ rather than constant 2015 US$, the level could move, but no current-US$ per-worker figure for Egypt was found in these pages.
answer.search_trail: Started at the World Bank indicator landing page for NV.AGR.EMPL.KD (Source 1), which carries an all-countries table; located the Egypt, Arab Rep. row with most recent year 2025 and value 8,942.42 and used that as the quote. Cross-checked the same value on the French mirror of the country-filtered page (Source 10, donnees.banquemondiale.org, tier-flagged T5 by domain but substantively the same World Bank series) which shows 8 942,42 for 2025 — used only as corroboration, not as the citation, since the .org data.worldbank.org page is the T1 original. Read both metadata glossary entries (Sources 2 and 3) to pin the sector scope (ISIC Rev. 4 divisions 01-03, i.e. agriculture plus forestry plus fishing) and the price basis (constant 2015 US$), which is what drives the construct_note. Checked the DataBank multi-year table (Source 4) for an Egypt time series, but the retrieved extract truncates alphabetically at Cambodia and never reaches Egypt, so no year-by-year Egypt values could be quoted from it. Checked the WDI table 3.3 extract (Source 5) for 2011 and 2019 Egypt values, but the text truncates mid-row at 'Egypt, Arab' before any figures, so nothing quotable there either. Looked for a national-source alternative: CAPMAS microdata catalogue entry for the Annual Bulletin of Agricultural Income Estimates 2016-2017 (Source 6) is a catalogue record only and publishes no per-worker productivity figure; the Ministry of Agriculture publications listing (Source 9) returns agronomy trial papers, no productivity statistics. answer.abstain_reason: No source in the retrieved set publishes an all-crop national post-harvest loss rate for Egypt. The only quantified Egyptian figures are (a) a wheat-only estimate of 20.62% of total supply lost OR WASTED across the whole value chain (i.e. including milling, distribution and household/consumption waste, not post-harvest loss alone, and including imported wheat), and (b) a T5 conference presentation reporting a 16-48% literature range for cereals plus an explicit author 'guesstimate' of 10%. Neither is a published measure of the named construct, and the two bodies of evidence straddle three different score bands (10% to 48% spans levels 1 to 4), so no level can be ratified.
answer.value: For Egypt no all-crop national post-harvest loss rate is published; the best quantified evidence is a peer-reviewed wheat value-chain study estimating that about 4.4 million tons, 20.62% of total wheat supply (domestic production plus imports) in 2017/2018, is lost or wasted, a figure that covers waste at consumption as well as losses after harvest, alongside a grey-literature report that published cereals-loss estimates for Egypt range from 16% to 48% with no authoritative national measurement.
answer.unit: percent of total wheat supply (loss and waste combined)
answer.source_title: Sustainability (MDPI), Yigezu et al., 'Food Losses and Wastage along the Wheat Value Chain in Egypt and Their Implications on Food and Energy Security, Natural Resources, and the Environment'
answer.quote: About 4.4 million tons (20.62% of total wheat supply from domestic production and imports in 2017/2018) is estimated to be lost or wasted in Egypt which is also associated with the wastage of about 4.79 billion m3 of water, and 74.72 million GJ of energy.
answer.data_quality_flag: Wheat-only value-chain study combining loss and waste; denominator includes imported wheat. Secondary range figure comes from a conference presentation citing 1970s literature and an explicit 'guesstimate'.
answer.construct_note: The indicator name asserts an all-crop national post-harvest loss rate. The best available Egyptian figure (20.62%) is (i) wheat only, not all crops; (ii) loss AND wastage across the full life cycle, so it includes retail and household food waste that falls outside 'post-harvest loss'; and (iii) computed over total supply including imports rather than over domestic harvested production. The COMCEC/NRI case study (T5) states for Egyptian cereals: 'Limited published literature on postharvest losses in Egypt. Literature from 1970's suggests a range of 16-48%' and that the authors 'made a guesstimate' of 10% postharvest loss for wheat, maize and rice - again cereals only, and self-described as a guess. CAPMAS bulletins define a loss term (الفاقد, quantities lost during sorting, packing, transport, storage and processing) inside the food-balance identity but the retrieved pages carry no percentage for it.
answer.quality_evidence: Source 6 is a peer-reviewed article applying standard measurement protocols along the wheat chain with primary survey data by ICARDA and Egypt's Agricultural Research Center - methodologically strong but scoped to one commodity and to loss-plus-waste. Source 9 is a presentation deck reporting no primary measurement for Egypt ('APHLIS does not cover North Africa', 'No data on economic losses reported'). Sources 1-5 (CAPMAS, T1) supply food-balance methodology and self-sufficiency ratios only.
answer.scale_evidence: National in coverage for wheat supply (domestic production plus imports, 2017/2018); no crop-weighted national aggregate across all commodities exists in the retrieved evidence.
answer.rung_argument: A level is withheld rather than argued. Were the wheat figure accepted at face value (20.62%), it would sit just below the 20 cut and yield level 2; the COMCEC 10% guesstimate would yield level 4; the upper end of the cited 16-48% literature range would yield level 1. Because the candidate figures cross three bands and none measures the named all-crop post-harvest construct, no rung can be established on the evidence supplied.
answer.negative_finding: Nothing in the retrieved pages reports an all-crop, harvest-to-market loss percentage for Egypt separated from consumption-stage waste, and no national statistical office or FAO/FLI country estimate for Egypt appears in the supplied set; without that, even level 1 would rest on a construct the sources do not measure.

Source 8 (Foods 2017, Kumar & Kalita) is a global developing-country review with no Egypt-specific rate in the retrieved text. 1.6.name: Smallholder access to formal markets (%)

answer.abstain_reason: None of the supplied pages publishes a figure for smallholder ACCESS to formal markets in Egypt. The closest evidence (IFPRI/AgEcon working paper on smallholder participation in profitable value chains and contract farming) measures a different construct — contract-farming/high-value-chain PARTICIPATION among sampled irrigated-agriculture households — and the retrieved text contains no percentage at all that could be quoted verbatim. The remaining pages are census/bulletin metadata (no market-access statistic) or project-output counts. No admissible, quote-verifiable figure exists in the retrieved material.
answer.construct_note: Indicator name asserts national smallholder ACCESS to formal markets, expressed as a percentage. The best available Egyptian evidence in these pages is Tabe-Ojong & Abay (IFPRI), 'Smallholder farmers' participation in profitable value chains and contract farming: Evidence from irrigated agriculture in Egypt', which estimates a multivariate probit of joint PARTICIPATION in value chains and contract farming among a survey sample of irrigated smallholders — participation in one contractual channel is not the same as access to formal markets, and the sample is regional (irrigated governorates), not national. Its only quotable general statement is that participation 'remains low in Africa', which is a continental, not Egyptian, claim. Contextual non-matching material: GIZ AIP industrial scan (T4) describes willingness of buyers to source from smallholders in six Upper Egypt governorates qualitatively with no rate; MALR's PRIME page (T3) reports programme outputs — 'Implementing marketing contracts for 42 thousand acres' and 'Forming 256 marketing committees for the small farmers' in seven governorates — which are project counts, not a share of smallholders with market access; GIZ Gender Value Chain Assessment lists a 'Selling point' figure for a 100-farmer Minya/Beni Suef sample, again neither national nor a published access percentage. None of these can substitute for the named construct.
answer.quality_evidence: The only peer-review-grade source (T2, AgEcon Search working paper by IFPRI authors) is methodologically sound but sample-based and regional; the retrieved text is limited to title page, abstract and introduction and contains no descriptive participation rate. T1 sources retrieved (FAO microdata catalogue entry for the 2009-2010 Agricultural Census; CAPMAS NADA catalogue and cooperative-activity bulletin front matter) are metadata/index pages only and carry no marketing or market-access statistic.
answer.scale_evidence: No national-scale measurement of smallholder market access was located. Available scale evidence is programmatic and subnational: PRIME covers seven governorates (Kafr Elshikh, Bohira, ELmnya, Beni suif, Qena, Asuit, Sohag) with 42,000 acres under marketing contracts; AIP works with 30 farmer organisations in Minya and Beni Suef. Neither provides a denominator of Egyptian smallholders.
answer.rung_argument: No level is proposed. A threshold indicator scored on a published percentage requires a percentage that measures the named construct for the named country; nothing in the retrieved pages supplies one, and the assessment's own census flags that the previously used Egyptian figure was a regional contract-farming participation rate rather than national market access. Scoring any rung from participation counts or project outputs would convert a data gap into a numeric claim.
answer.negative_finding: Even the lowest rung (below the 20 cut) is withheld because the evidence does not establish any measured share of Egyptian smallholders with formal-market access — not a low one and not a high one. The specific missing item is a nationally representative survey or official statistic reporting the proportion of Egyptian smallholders selling through formal channels (contracts, cooperatives, registered wholesale/export buyers, organised retail); no such published proportion appears in the supplied material.

1.7.name: Agricultural credit access (% farmers)

answer.abstain_reason: None of the retrieved pages publish a share (percentage) of farmers — or of any farming population — with access to agricultural credit in Egypt. The only Egypt-specific credit evidence retrieved is monetary loan volume (CAPMAS agricultural cooperative bulletins, Forbes MENA reporting on CAPMAS investment-loan totals) and a catalogue of Agricultural Bank of Egypt loan products with eligibility terms. These are denominators-free flow measures, not a proportion of farmers. Converting them into a percentage would require an assumption about the farmer denominator that no supplied source makes.
answer.construct_note: The indicator names a SHARE OF FARMERS with credit ACCESS. The best Egypt evidence in the supplied pages is (a) CAPMAS annual bulletins of agricultural cooperative activity, which tabulate the VALUE of in-kind and cash loans granted by season and governorate and the benefitted AREA (feddans), not the number or share of farmers served; (b) Forbes Middle East reporting CAPMAS figures that investment loans to farmers and agribusiness rose to EGP 56 billion in FY2023-24 — again a monetary total; (c) a Ministry of Environment green-finance page listing Agricultural Bank of Egypt product terms (e.g. crop loans of EGP 2,000–10,000 for small farmers), which describes supply-side offer, not uptake or coverage. Separately, the census note for this row flags that Egypt's previously recorded figure came from Findex-style 'rural adults aged 15+' borrowing, which is both a different population (includes non-farmers) and a different concept (borrowing/use rather than access); no such Findex page was supplied here either, so it cannot be quote-verified. The FAO World Census of Agriculture page for Egypt 1999/2000 gives 4,541,884 holdings, which would be a plausible denominator but the supplied pages contain no matching count of credit-receiving farmers, so no ratio can be formed.
answer.quality_evidence: CAPMAS agricultural cooperative bulletins (T1) are annual and governorate-disaggregated but report loan value and benefitted area, with no borrower headcount in the retrieved text; the retrieved English summary bulletin is also heavily digit-stripped by extraction, so even the monetary figures could not be quoted reliably as numbers. The FAO holdings count (T2, openknowledge.fao.org) is from the 1999/2000 census and carries no credit variable in the retrieved extract. The Forbes item is T5 and may not be used for a statistic. The ScienceDirect article on smallholder agricultural credit constraints returned a captcha page, so nothing in it could be read or quoted.
answer.scale_evidence: No population-scaled measure of credit access was retrievable. Supply-side scale is indicated only in currency terms (EGP 56 billion of investment loans in FY2023-24, per a T5 report of CAPMAS data) and by product ceilings (crop loans EGP 2,000–10,000; mechanization loans up to EGP 250,000 for individuals), none of which establishes how many of Egypt's roughly 4.5 million holdings are reached.
answer.rung_argument: No level is proposed. A threshold indicator scored against cut points of 10, 25, 40 and 60 percent requires a published percentage for the named construct; the supplied evidence contains no percentage of any farming population. Placing this cell at level 1 would falsely assert that measured coverage is below 10 percent, and placing it higher would falsely assert a measured share the sources do not contain. The honest record is a ratification hold pending either a Findex-derived rural/farmer borrowing figure (which would itself require the construct question in the census note to be settled) or a CAPMAS/ABE disclosure of borrower counts against a farmer denominator.
answer.negative_finding: No level, including level 1, is supported: the evidence does not establish any measured share of Egyptian farmers with agricultural credit access, only loan values, loan product terms, and benefitted cultivated area. Level 1 would require a published figure below 10 percent for the named construct, and no such figure appears in the supplied pages.
answer.search_trail: Worked through the ten supplied pages in tier order. (1) CAPMAS censusinfo bulletin on investment loans to farmers — read fully; it reports totals in billion pounds by loan maturity, with the extracted text's digits largely stripped; no farmer counts or percentages. (2) and (3) CAPMAS Annual Bulletin of agricultural sector cooperative activity 2016/17 and 2017/18 — read prefaces and full table indexes; every loan table is 'value of in-kind and in cash loans granted ... and the benefitted areas', i.e. money and feddans by governorate, plus association membership counts; no table promises borrowers as a share of farmers. (4) CAPMAS agriculture subject landing page — navigation shell only, no data. (5) CAPMAS Zemam and agricultural ownership bulletin overview — land area and ownership metadata, no credit variable. (6) FAO World Census of Agriculture, Egypt 1999/2000 — checked for a credit or 'holdings reporting credit' block; the extract covers holdings, tenure, employment, land use, crops, livestock and machinery, but contains no credit item; noted the 4,541,884 holdings figure only as a potential denominator. (7) ScienceDirect 'Agricultural credit constraints in smallholder farming' — blocked by captcha, nothing readable, dead end. (8) and (9) Ministry of Environment CLEI green-finance pages for the Agricultural Bank of Egypt (English and Arabic) — full product catalogue with amounts, tenors and interest rates; supply-side terms only, no uptake or coverage share. (10) Forbes Middle East on Egypt's farm credit — T5, reports CAPMAS investment-loan totals of EGP 56 billion for FY2023-24; useful context but a T5 page may not carry a statistic and in any case reports value, not farmer share. Searched all pages for the words 'percent', '%', 'share of farmers' and 'access to credit' in the credit context; the only percentages present are interest rates, financing ratios (80%, 25-70% of production costs) and year-on-year growth rates. Conclusion: the named construct is not published in any supplied page for Egypt.

1.8.name: Farmers using climate-smart practices (%)

answer.abstain_reason: None of the retrieved pages publishes a percentage of farmers in Egypt using climate-smart practices. The available evidence measures adjacent but different constructs (climate-change awareness among farmers in two Delta governorates; qualitative descriptions of adaptation intensity across seven governorates; share of WHEAT AREA under mechanised raised-bed farming in Sharkia; a project target of 8,000 farmers to be reached by 2027) and none is a national farmer-level adoption share. Recording any of these as the indicator value would substitute a different construct and a sub-national scope for the named one.
answer.construct_note: Closest evidence: (a) Kassem et al. 2019 (Sustainability, via DigitalCommons@USU) surveyed 792 farmers in two Nile Delta governorates and reports that 51.9% had NO knowledge of the climate change phenomenon, with manure use, changed crop patterns and crop rotation the commonest adaptation measures among the aware minority — this is an awareness statistic for two governorates, not a national share of farmers using climate-smart practices; (b) Swelam et al. 2026 (Sci Rep, 2953 farmers, seven governorates) reports qualitatively 'limited uptake of technical adaptation measures' concentrated on 'low-cost, incremental practices' with modern irrigation and digital tools 'rarely adopted' — no adoption percentage is given; (c) the ICARDA/AFESD technical report tabulates the 'Relative Importance of Wheat Areas under MRB Farming in Sharkia Governorate' — a share of AREA under one practice in one governorate, which is the exact land-vs-farmers, single-practice, sub-national mismatch flagged in the indicator census; (d) the FAO SHARP+ project page states a forward-looking target that 'over 8,000 farmers will adopt climate-smart agriculture and biodiversity-friendly practices across 3,000 hectares' by 2027 — a project target, not a denominator-based national share. Egypt has roughly 4-5 million agricultural holders, so 8,000 is not convertible to a meaningful national percentage.
answer.quality_evidence: The two peer-reviewed farmer surveys (n=792 and n=2953) are methodologically credible for their sampled governorates but neither reports an adoption rate for a defined basket of climate-smart practices, and neither is nationally representative. The FAO technical book 'Towards climate-smart agriculture in Egypt' (2022) is a practice-documentation study based on field visits, explicitly qualitative in its synopsis ('examines a number of interventions and practices... analyses the extent to which they contribute to the three CSA pillars'), with no adoption-rate statistic in the retrieved record page.
answer.scale_evidence: Scale evidence is fragmentary and non-comparable: an 8,000-farmer / 3,000-hectare project target (FAO GCP/EGY/039/CAN, 2023-2027); an unquantified (in the retrieved text) share of Sharkia wheat area under mechanised raised beds 2013-2017; and survey-based awareness/adaptation profiles for two and seven governorates respectively. No national denominator-based measure was located.
answer.rung_argument: No level is proposed. A threshold score requires a published value for the named construct — the percentage of Egyptian farmers using climate-smart practices. The retrieved pages contain no such value, and the nearest figures measure awareness (51.9% unaware, two governorates), area under one practice (Sharkia wheat), or a project beneficiary target. Scoring level 1 from the qualitative 'limited uptake' finding would be an inference from a non-representative sample across a differently-defined practice basket, and scoring anything higher would be unsupported; either would convert a data gap into an assessed value.
answer.negative_finding: Not applicable — no level proposed. The specific missing item is any nationally scoped, farmer-denominated adoption rate for a defined set of climate-smart practices in Egypt, from a statistical office, FAO/World Bank database, or nationally representative survey.

8.1.name: Prevalence of undernourishment (%)

answer.source_title: World Bank Open Data (WDI), Prevalence of undernourishment (% of population) — Egypt, Arab Rep. (source: FAO)
answer.quote: Egypt, Arab Rep.	2023	9
answer.data_quality_flag: FAO model-based estimate derived from food balance sheets and household consumption distributions; World Bank portal displays the figure rounded to whole percent (the underlying FAO series value for 2023 is reported elsewhere as 9.4)
answer.construct_note: The World Bank series SN.ITK.DEFC.ZS is FAO's SDG indicator 2.1.1, prevalence of undernourishment as a percentage of the national population — exactly the named construct, for Egypt, Arab Rep.
answer.quality_evidence: Value comes from the FAO Suite of Food Security Indicators as republished in the World Bank's WDI country page for Egypt, Arab Rep. FAO's SDG portal (Source 4) confirms the definition: 'an estimate of the proportion of the population whose habitual food consumption is insufficient to provide the dietary energy levels that are required to maintain a normal active and healthy life. It is expressed as a percentage.' PoU is a three-year-averaged modelled estimate, not a direct survey measurement, which is a methodological caveat rather than a construct mismatch.
answer.scale_evidence: National-population coverage for Egypt; most recent year available in the series is 2023, with the series spanning 2001-2023 on the same page.
answer.rung_argument: The recorded figure is 9 percent for Egypt (2023), taken verbatim from a T1 publisher (World Bank/WDI) republishing the FAO custodian series for SDG 2.1.1. Construct: the indicator name and the source series are the same construct (prevalence of undernourishment, % of population), so no substitution or proxying was needed. Coverage: national, matching the indicator's implied national scope. Currency: 2023 is the latest reference year in the series. Applying the threshold ladder (lower is better) to a value of 9: it is below the 25 cut and below the 15 cut, placing it above the bottom two bands; it is not below the 7.5 cut, so it sits in the 7.5-15 band, i.e. level 3.
answer.negative_finding: Level 4 would require a prevalence below 7.5 percent. Egypt's published 2023 value is 9 (9.4 in the finer-grained FAO series shown on TheGlobalEconomy's reproduction), which is above 7.5, and the series on the World Bank page is rising rather than falling toward that cut (the y-axis on the Egypt chart runs to 10.0 and the most recent value is the series maximum). Nothing in the supplied pages shows an Egyptian PoU figure under 7.5 for any recent year.
answer.search_trail: 1) World Bank WDI Egypt page for SN.ITK.DEFC.ZS (T1): gives 'Egypt, Arab Rep. 2023 9' in both the selected-country and all-countries tables — used as the recorded value. 2) FAO SOFI 2025 statistical tables (Source 2) and SOFI 2024 tables (Source 7): only notes and source statements were retrieved; the actual Table A1.1 country rows (and therefore Egypt's PoU) are not present in the supplied text, so no quotable Egypt figure there. 3) FAO SDG data portal 2.1.1 page (Source 4): definitional and global/regional figures only (7.8% global 2025, Africa 20.0%); no Egypt-specific value. 4) UNSD SDG country profile page (Source 5): the URL is countryprofiles/mdg — Madagascar, not Egypt (33.4% in 2001 to 39.5% in 2023). Explicitly rejected under the do-not-cross-borders rule; those figures are NOT Egypt's. 5) CAPMAS metadata catalogue (Source 3): a study landing page for 'Economics of food security in Egypt 2006-2015' with no figures in the retrieved text. 6) World Bank 'Scaling Up Nutrition in Egypt' (Source 6): only front matter retrieved, no PoU figure. 7) PMC article (Source 8): child malnutrition co-occurrence, a different construct. 8) TheGlobalEconomy (Source 9, T5): reports 9.4 percent for 2023 citing FAO — consistent with the World Bank value but T5 may not carry a statistic, so it is used only as corroboration of rounding, not as the source of record.

8.5.name: Women who own land (% holders)

answer.abstain_reason: The only figure in the supplied pages for women's share of agricultural land in Egypt (4 percent female holders, from the 2009/2010 agricultural census) appears solely on a T5 page (a conference presentation slide deck hosted on arablandinitiative.gltn.net), and T5 sources may be used for existence facts only, never for a statistic. In addition, that figure counts agricultural HOLDERS (operators, who may rent rather than own), not women who OWN land, which is the construct named by this indicator. No T1-T4 page among those retrieved carries a quotable figure: the CAPMAS catalogue entries (Sources 1, 2, 4) are metadata landing pages with no sex-disaggregated values, the FAO microdata entry (Source 3) is census documentation only, the FAO GLRD page (Source 5) returned a 404, the FAOSTAT catalogue entry (Source 6) describes the 'sex of agricultural holders' variable without publishing Egypt's value, the FAO/CIHEAM small-scale family farming study (Source 7) shows only a table of contents including section '1.2.6 Gender composition of the holders' with no numeric text supplied, and the FAO Country Gender Assessment brief (Source 8) and GIZ GVCA report (Source 9) supply narrative and figure titles but no extractable national percentage in the retrieved text.
answer.construct_note: Context only, not recorded as the cell value: a T5 slide deck ('Women's land rights in Arab countries', GLTN Arab Land Initiative) tabulates FAO World Programme for the Census of Agriculture 2010 results giving Egypt (census 2009/2012) 5401432 total holders, of whom 212779 (4%) are female holders operating 114694 ha (3%) of area. Two problems sit on top of each other. First, tier: the page is T5, which is admissible for existence facts but never for a statistic, so this number cannot be ratified from the evidence supplied. Second, construct: 'holder' is defined on that same page, per Eurostat, as the person on whose account and in whose name the holding is operated and who bears the economic risk - the holder 'can own the holding outright or rent it or be a hereditary long-term leaseholder or a usufructuary or a trustee'. That is operatorship, not ownership. The indicator as NAMED asks for women who OWN land, so the canonical holder statistic sits on the wrong side of the unratified definitional question flagged in the indicator census. A ratified owner-based figure would need to come from a land-ownership or asset-ownership survey (e.g. SDG 5.a.1, or CAPMAS agricultural property/'zemam' ownership tabulations), none of which are present in numeric form in the retrieved pages.
answer.rung_argument: No level proposed. A threshold level here would have to rest either on a quotable figure at an admissible tier or on a body of evidence that brackets the cut points (10, 25, 40, 50). Neither is available in the supplied pages. The 4 percent holder figure, if it were both admissible and construct-matched, would fall below the first cut point and imply level 1, but it is neither: it is T5-only and it measures operatorship rather than ownership. Proposing level 1 on that basis would launder a tier-inadmissible, construct-mismatched number into a scored row, which is the failure mode this rubric is built to prevent. Withholding the level is the correct outcome.
answer.negative_finding: No level was proposed at all, so no next rung applies. The specific missing item is a T1-T4 published figure, for Egypt, for the share of land OWNERS (or landholding-title holders) who are women - or, failing that, an admissible-tier restatement of the census holder share that the assessment could ratify as a proxy after resolving the owner-versus-holder definitional question.
answer.search_trail: Worked through the ten supplied pages in tier order. Source 1 and Source 2 (CAPMAS censusinfo, T1, Agricultural Property and Rein 2017 and 2015): catalogue landing pages listing downloadable press releases, a bulletin and tables, but the retrieved text contains no sex-disaggregated ownership values - the underlying PDFs were not supplied. Source 4 (CAPMAS Arabic 'zemam and agricultural ownership' bulletin overview, T1): abstract and keywords cover total zemam, government and private lands and 'المساحة المملوكة' (owned area), but the unit of analysis is stated as feddans and no gender breakdown appears; this is the most likely home for an Egyptian owner-based figure and is the gap to close on a rerun. Source 3 (FAO microdata, Egypt Agricultural Census 2009-2010, T1): methodology metadata only; scope lists holding characteristics and employment, no published results table. Source 5 (FAO Gender and Land Rights Database, T1): the deep link returned a 404 error page, so the GLRD Egypt country profile - the natural custodian for this indicator - could not be read. Source 6 (FAOSTAT structural data from agricultural censuses, T1): confirms the domain disseminates 'sex of agricultural holders' as a percentage of holdings, but the catalogue page itself carries no Egypt value; the actual data download was not fetched. Source 7 (FAO/CIHEAM/CIRAD small-scale family farming in Egypt, T2): the retrieved text stops at the table of contents, which lists '1.2.6 Gender composition of the holders' on page 20 - the figure is very likely there but is not in the text supplied, so quoting it would be fabrication. Source 8 (FAO Country Gender Assessment of the Agriculture and Rural Sector: Egypt, T2): retrieved text is front matter plus the opening of 'Main findings', all qualitative on invisibility and structural barriers; no land-ownership percentage in the supplied extract. Source 9 (GIZ Gender Value Chain Assessment, T4): the list of figures includes 'Figure 2: Land ownership by gender', but this is a 100-farmer purposive sample in Minya and Beni Suef, i.e. sub-national and non-representative even if the numbers had been supplied, which they were not. Source 10 (GLTN Arab Land Initiative presentation, T5): the only page carrying an actual Egypt number - 212779 female holders, 4 percent - rejected on tier and on the holder-versus-owner construct as set out in construct_note. Dead ends: no SDG 5.a.1 reporting, no Demographic and Health Survey asset-ownership module, and no CAPMAS ownership tabulation by sex appeared among the retrieved pages.

8.5.perplexity_lead:
No source publishes this exact indicator “women who own land (% holders)” for Egypt in the precise form you describe (i.e., the share of all *land holders* who both hold and *own* land, restricted to women), so there is a construct mismatch between the indicator name and the closest available statistics.

Below are the closest **published** measures, with notes on how they diverge from your requested construct:

- **Women who own land – individual women as owners (not % of holders):**  
  Several sources report that **about 2% of Egyptian women own land**, based on 2014 survey data used by UN Women and FAO.[2][3][7][10] These are proportions of *women in the population* who own land, not “% of land holders who are women owners,” so they do **not** directly answer a “% holders” question, but they do match the ownership aspect of the construct against the *population* denominator rather than holders.

- **Women’s share of land ownership – % of land area or owners that is female-owned:**  
  Multiple assessments state that **5.2% of agricultural land in Egypt is owned by women**, a figure attributed to FAO and used by FAO, GIZ and others.[2][3][9][13]

The only Egypt-specific coverage figures available are ITU national totals (at least 3G, at least LTE/WiMAX), which measure a different construct than the rural coverage named by this indicator. The ITU Facts and Figures 2025 page carries urban/rural splits only at world, income-group and region level, not for Egypt. answer.source_title: ITU DataHub, Population coverage, by mobile network technology (Egypt)
answer.data_quality_flag: ITU country coverage values are operator-reported/modelled national estimates with no urban-rural disaggregation published at country level
answer.construct_note: The indicator names RURAL coverage. The best available Egypt-specific evidence is NATIONAL: ITU DataHub reports for Egypt, 2025, 'At least 3G 99.8%', 'At least LTE/WiMAX 98%', 'At least 2G 99.9%', 'At least 5G 11%' (% of individuals). These are whole-population figures and cannot be read as rural coverage: ITU's own 2025 Facts and Figures shows that the uncovered residual is 'exclusively rural', so a national figure systematically overstates the rural value by construction. This cell therefore sits on the wrong side of the census's open question: recording the ITU national at-least-3G number here would mechanically score level 5 for a rural construct that no source has measured for Egypt. ITU's global/regional rural numbers (e.g. 4G covering 84 per cent of rural areas worldwide; Arab States 5G 13 per cent) are aggregates, not Egypt values, and rule 5 forbids importing them.
answer.quality_evidence: T1 ITU DataHub is the correct publisher tier for this construct and does publish urban/rural coverage series globally (the ITU Statistics landing page advertises 'Population covered by a mobile-cellular and a mobile-broadband network, total and by urban/rural area' as a global/regional time series), but no Egypt-level rural breakdown appears in any page retrieved. answer.scale_evidence: None available for the rural construct in Egypt. National scale context only: at least 3G 99.8% and at least LTE/WiMAX 98% of individuals in 2025 (ITU DataHub, Egypt).
answer.rung_argument: No level is proposed. A threshold level here would have to rest on a published rural coverage percentage for Egypt; the only quotable Egypt number measures national coverage. Scoring the national 99.8% against the 20/40/60/80 cut points would award level 5 to a construct for which no measurement exists, which is precisely the failure mode flagged in the indicator census. The honest record is a ratification hold until either (a) the register redefines this row as national at-least-3G coverage, in which case the ITU DataHub value is directly quotable and admissible, or (b) an ITU/MCIT rural-disaggregated figure for Egypt is located.
answer.negative_finding: Not applicable in the usual sense because no level is claimed; the specific gap is that no source states what share of Egypt's RURAL population is within range of a 3G or 4G signal. answer.source_title: ITU DataHub, Egypt ICT prices dashboard (IPB)
answer.data_quality_flag: Retrieved pages are client-side-rendered dashboards; the underlying data table did not render into the captured text.
answer.construct_note: The indicator name 'Mobile broadband price (% GNI pc)' does not fix the basket. The supplied ITU pages confirm that from the 2025 collection ITU publishes at least three candidate mobile series for each economy — 'Data-only mobile broadband basket 5 GB, as a % of GNI pc', 'Mobile broadband data and voice low-consumption basket total (70 min, 50 SMS, 1 GB), as a % of monthly GNI per capita', and 'Mobile broadband data and voice high-consumption basket total (140 min, 20 SMS, 5 GB), % GNI p.c.' — and that the pre-2025 methodology (in force 2021-2024, with the 2GB data-only basket) has been retired to a legacy/temporary-collection status ('Temporary data collection: The Mobile-broadband data and voice high-consumption basket, according to the 2021-2024 definition'). Any Egypt value must therefore be tagged with which of these baskets it comes from before it can be compared with another country's value; the census's open question is confirmed by these sources but not resolved by them. Note also that ITU's denominator convention here is MONTHLY GNI per capita (the Broadband Commission target is 'entry-level broadband services costing less than 2 per cent of monthly GNI per capita'), whereas the indicator name says only '% GNI pc'.
answer.quality_evidence: ITU is the T1 authority for this construct and the supplied methodology manual (ITU ICT Price Basket Statistics Manual, January 2025) documents the basket definitions and the step-by-step calculation, so a defensible figure is obtainable in principle. What is missing is the country datum itself.
answer.scale_evidence: None. No Egypt-specific price, GNI-per-capita denominator, or basket percentage appears in any supplied page.
answer.rung_argument: No level is proposed. The threshold cuts (10, 5, 2, 1) can only be applied to a published Egypt figure for a specified mobile-broadband basket as a percentage of GNI per capita. No such figure appears in the retrieved pages, so every rung is unsupported: I cannot even establish that Egypt's value is below 10, because the evidence set contains no Egyptian price observation at all.
answer.negative_finding: Level 1 (value below 10 % of GNI pc) is not proposed because the supplied sources contain no Egypt data point whatsoever — only dashboard chrome, basket-name menu labels, and methodology text. 2.7.name: Rural smartphone ownership (%)

answer.abstain_reason: The only figure in the supplied pages that touches rural smartphone ownership in Egypt is carried by a T5 news outlet (Ahram Online) reporting a CAPMAS 2015 HIECS result. Tier rules permit T5 for existence facts only, never for a statistic, so the figure cannot be ratified from this page; no T1/T2/T3 page among those retrieved carries a rural-disaggregated smartphone ownership figure. The figure is also a HOUSEHOLD measure ('families own smartphones'), which sits on the wrong side of the unratified individual-vs-household definition question, and it is a 2015 reference year, now a decade stale.
answer.source_title: Ahram Online, '88.1 pct of Egyptian families own mobile phones: CAPMAS'
answer.data_quality_flag: Only available rural figure is second-hand news reporting of a 2015 CAPMAS survey; the primary CAPMAS HIECS 2015 table was not retrieved, so the number cannot be verified against the statistical office publication.
answer.construct_note: Context only, not ratified: the Ahram Online report of the CAPMAS 2015 Household Income, Expenditure and Consumption Survey states that in rural areas 13.9 percent of families own smartphones (versus 31.7 percent urban and 22.1 percent nationally). Two mismatches with the indicator as named: (a) it is the share of rural HOUSEHOLDS owning at least one smartphone, not the share of rural INDIVIDUALS owning a personal smartphone — exactly the open definitional question the indicator census flags, and the household measure reads systematically higher than the individual one; (b) the publisher of the page carrying the number is a news outlet (T5), which is not an admissible tier for a statistic. The MCIT 'ICT Indicators in Brief' pages (T3) carry only national mobile subscription and penetration series (e.g. mobile penetration 98.34% and 105.01 million subscriptions in August 2023) with no rural/urban disaggregation and no smartphone-specific ownership measure; the only rural item there is 'Number of Local Exchanges in Rural Areas' (1072), a fixed-line infrastructure count.
answer.quality_evidence: CAPMAS is the national statistical office and the HIECS is a large probability sample (~25,000 households per the news account), so the underlying survey would be T1-grade if the CAPMAS table itself were in hand. The CAPMAS metadata pages retrieved (censusinfo.capmas.gov.eg) are for the 2011 Basic ICT Indicators household survey; its data dictionary contains an urban/rural code (r_u_code) and a mobile ownership variable (mobile), but the pages retrieved publish only unweighted record counts for unrelated variables, with an explicit warning that the counts are not weighted and cannot be interpreted as representative of the population. No smartphone variable and no rural cross-tabulation appear in those pages.
answer.scale_evidence: No admissible rural smartphone ownership statistic could be quoted, so no scale claim is recorded. For orientation only, national mobile penetration reported by MCIT was 98.34% in August 2023 (subscriptions, not persons, and not smartphones), and mobile internet users were 74.57 million.
answer.rung_argument: No level is proposed. The threshold cuts (20/40/60/80) can only be applied to a figure that measures rural smartphone ownership at an admissible tier. The single candidate figure (13.9% of rural families, CAPMAS HIECS 2015) fails on tier (quoted only from a news page) and on construct (households, not individuals). Assigning level 1 on the strength of it would silently ratify a 2015 household statistic sourced from a newspaper as the country's rural individual smartphone ownership rate, and would also be defensibly wrong in the other direction: individual ownership in 2024-25 is almost certainly far above the 2015 household figure, so an arithmetic level 1 would understate as badly as a national figure would overstate.
answer.negative_finding: What is missing for any level above withheld: a CAPMAS, ITU, GSMA Consumer Survey or Findex table that reports, for Egypt, the share of rural respondents (individuals) who own a smartphone, published by the statistical office or an admissible T1-T4 publisher and quotable from the page itself. Nothing in the retrieved pages disaggregates smartphone ownership by rural residence at an admissible tier; the MCIT briefs stop at national subscription counts and the CAPMAS metadata pages stop at unweighted variable frequencies for the 2011 survey.
answer.search_trail: 1) CAPMAS microdata catalogue (censusinfo.capmas.gov.eg), EGY-CAPMAS-BEIMIS-2011 'Basic ICT Indicators for Measuring the Information Society (Household) 2011' — checked the F1 (Telecommunications) and F8 (General Indicators) data dictionaries and two variable pages (V13, V17). The file carries r_u_code (urban/rural) and 'mobile' / 'mobile_no' variables, but no smartphone variable, and the published category tables are unweighted record counts with an explicit non-representativeness warning. Dead end for the named construct. 2) The 2006/2011 questionnaire PDF (download/592) — contains a household question on third-generation-enabled mobiles and mobile internet use, but is an instrument, not results, and carries no rural tabulation. There is **no published source in the retrieved material that reports “rural smartphone ownership (%)” for individuals in Egypt**, and thus the specific indicator you ask for cannot be directly answered. All relevant evidence refers to **rural households** owning smartphones, not rural individuals.

### 1. Does any source publish “rural smartphone ownership (%)” for individuals?

No. None of the sources found report the **proportion of rural individuals** in Egypt who personally own a smartphone. Available figures either:

- Combine urban and rural into a single national figure; or  
- Report **household-level** smartphone ownership in rural areas.

Because your indicator name explicitly specifies **RURAL** and implicitly refers to **individual ownership of a personal device**, these available measures are **construct mismatches**, not valid answers.

### 2. Best available evidence (construct mismatch) and what it says

The closest match is a **household-level** statistic from Egypt’s official statistics agency (CAPMAS), reported by Ahram Online based on the 2015 Household Income, Expenditure and Consumption Survey:

- Nationally, **22.1% of Egyptian families own smartphones**.[1]

2.11.name: Device financing/subsidy schemes

answer.value: Egypt has a publicly backed device financing scheme: the ProGIG Initiative, run jointly by the Ministry of Communications and Information Technology's National Telecommunication Institute (NTI) and Nasser Social Bank, offering soft loans of up to EGP 65,000 with a 50% discount on administrative costs over two years for the purchase of laptops by graduates and trainees of MCIT programmes; no farmer- or rural-targeted device financing or subsidy scheme was found in the retrieved sources, and the only handset-financing volumes located are commercial consumer-finance instalments reported in the trade press.
answer.source_title: Ministry of Communications and Information Technology (Egypt) — NTI: ProGIG Initiative
answer.quote: ProGIG is a joint initiative by the National Telecommunication Institute (NTI) and Nasser Social Bank (NSB) to support young people through soft loans for purchasing laptops.
answer.data_quality_flag: Implementer's own programme page; no publication date, no uptake or disbursement reporting
answer.construct_note: ProGIG is a state-backed device financing scheme with an embedded subsidy element (soft loans, 50% discount on administrative costs), so it sits on the 'subsidy present' side of the unresolved definitional question. However, its targeting is ICT trainees and graduates of MCIT programmes and the device financed is a laptop — not smartphones, and not farmers or rural households. The other class of evidence flagged in the indicator census — commercial handset instalments — also exists in Egypt but only in a T5 news report of Financial Regulatory Authority data (EGP 4.6bn of mobile-phone financing and 10.8 million consumer-finance clients in 2025), which is a market-wide commercial credit statistic with no public subsidy and no agricultural or rural targeting, and is not admissible here as a statistic. If the ratified definition requires a subsidy and/or agricultural targeting, the ProGIG evidence would satisfy the subsidy test but fail a rural/agricultural targeting test.
answer.rung_argument: Absent is ruled out: a named device financing instrument exists and is published by a government ministry (MCIT/NTI ProGIG). Announced is exceeded: the page does not merely signal intent, it states an operating partnership with a named financing institution (Nasser Social Bank) and fixed, adopted terms — a ceiling of EGP 65,000, a 50% discount on administrative costs, and a two-year term, with an eligibility population defined as graduates and participants of MCIT training programmes. That constitutes an adopted instrument with settled parameters, giving base level 3. I did not claim Operating over Adopted because no disbursement, enrolment or loan-issuance evidence was retrieved; in any case both rungs score 3.
answer.negative_finding: Level 4 was not proposed because `quality_evidence` is empty: the only source for ProGIG is the implementing ministry's own descriptive page, which states what the scheme offers but contains no evaluation, audit, performance report or service standard. Level 5 was not proposed because `scale_evidence` is also empty: no beneficiary counts, loan volumes or geographic coverage for ProGIG are published in the retrieved pages. The large handset-instalment figures in the retrieved trade-press item (banker.news, T5) belong to the commercial consumer-finance market supervised by the Financial Regulatory Authority, not to any subsidy scheme, and T5 material may not be used to carry a statistic.

Then checked whether any agriculture- or rural-targeted device scheme appeared: CAPMAS microdata catalogue entries (HIECS 2015 and 2021, the 2011 ICT household indicators survey, the 2014-15 telecommunications bulletin) were all household-survey metadata on ownership/expenditure and contain no reference to any financing or subsidy scheme for devices — dead ends for this construct. The two CGSpace/IFPRI items retrieved on Egyptian subsidy targeting (food ration proxy means tests, 2002; Takaful and Karama PMT targeting, 2018) concern food subsidies and cash transfers, not device acquisition — also dead ends. The banker.news item reports FRA consumer-finance statistics on mobile-phone instalment purchases in 2025; this is commercial credit, a T5 publisher, and cannot supply a statistic, so it is recorded only as context in construct_note. No page in the retrieved set documents a farmer- or rural-targeted device financing or subsidy scheme.

3.3.name: National farmer registry

gates.reason: The indicator names a registry of FARMERS (individuals). The only national instrument evidenced here is منظومة الحيازة الإلكترونية / كارت الفلاح — an electronic register of agricultural HOLDINGS and their holders (الحائزين), embedded in an input-subsidy smart-card scheme, with the national ID number used as the reference key for card issuance. It is therefore a holding registry with a person-level card layer, and its published scale figures mix four units (forms registered, cards printed and approved, target cards, holders enumerated), exactly the ambiguity flagged in the indicator census. Adjacent instruments examined that are NOT registries: the decennial Agricultural Census 2009-2010 (statistical enumeration of holdings, unit of analysis households, FAO microdata catalogue) and CAPMAS's نشرة الزمام والملكية الزراعية (land-tenure/ownership bulletin) — both are periodic statistical outputs, not maintained administrative registers.

answer.value: Egypt's nearest national instrument to a farmer registry is the Ministry of Agriculture and Land Reclamation's electronic agricultural-holding system "كارت الفلاح" (Farmer Card), keyed to the national ID number, under which 3.14 million holder registration forms had been recorded and 2.6 million cards printed and approved as of April 2019, with activation of the system stated as pending; the registered unit is the agricultural holder/holding, not an individual-farmer register as the indicator name implies.

gates.reason: rung Absent: the citation evidences the search, not the construct

answer.value: Egypt publishes agricultural statistics through several government channels — CAPMAS's NADA microdata catalogue (47 studies in the Agriculture collection, filterable only as 'Licensed data files' or 'Data not available'), the Ministry of Agriculture and Land Reclamation Economic Affairs Sector's on-screen crop/livestock query databases (agri.gov.eg), and PDF bulletins on moa.gov.eg — but none of these constitutes an open, openly licensed, bulk machine-readable and AI-ready agricultural data resource: the CAPMAS catalogue is login-gated with restrictive access conditions and no open licence, the MALR databases return HTML query tables (series ending 2019) with no documented bulk download or API, and the ministry's releases are PDFs; the only downloadable consolidated machine-readable agricultural dataset identified for Egypt, SPADE, is built and hosted by IFPRI/CGIAR rather than by an Egyptian public open-data instrument.
answer.source_title: CAPMAS Central Data Catalog — Egypt - Agricultural Property and Rein 2017 - Data Access
answer.quote: It is prohibited to publish or quote without reference to the source,CAPMAS
answer.data_quality_flag: Nearest adjacent instrument is a metadata catalogue whose Agriculture entries are marked either 'Licensed data files' or 'Data not available'; no open licence or bulk/API access documented on the retrieved pages.
answer.construct_note: The indicator names three conjoined qualifiers — open, machine-readable, AI-ready. The best national evidence retrieved (the CAPMAS NADA microdata catalogue) satisfies none of them in the sense the name requires: it is login-gated, its Agriculture holdings are flagged 'Licensed data files' or 'Data not available', and its access conditions restrict republication. This is exactly the wrong-side-of-the-question artifact flagged in the indicator census for Nigeria (a registration-gated statistical microdata catalogue scored as 'Operating with quality'); scoring Egypt's equivalent catalogue as the construct would repeat that error, so it is cited here only as evidence that the named instrument is not present. The IFPRI/CGIAR SPADE database (T2, over 1000 spatial datasets and layers, user-downloadable) is machine-readable and closer to the construct, but it is a research-organisation product consolidating already-public data, not an Egyptian open agricultural data instrument; the same IFPRI note records that in Egypt 'only a fraction is made publicly available'.
answer.rung_argument: Absent: I examined the three places a national open, machine-readable, AI-ready agricultural data instrument would sit — the national statistical office's data catalogue (CAPMAS NADA, Agriculture collection, 47 studies), the line ministry's own database section (MALR Economic Affairs Sector, قواعد البيانات / الانتاج النباتي), and the ministry's publications register — and none is an open data portal: CAPMAS requires login and imposes republication conditions with files licensed or unavailable, MALR offers a form-driven HTML table with no download, licence or API and series stopping at 2019, and moa.gov.eg offers PDF bulletins. Announced was not reached because no retrieved page contains a government announcement, policy commitment or roadmap for opening agricultural data in machine-readable form. Adopted and Operating therefore also fail: there is no adopted open-data licence, catalogue or API for agricultural data to point to, and nothing operating that meets the named qualifiers.
answer.negative_finding: Announced (level 2) was not proposed because none of the retrieved government pages — MALR databases, MALR publications, CAPMAS catalogue and access-policy pages — contains any statement of intent, policy, decree or programme to publish agricultural data as open, machine-readable or AI-ready resources; the only forward-looking language retrieved is a T2 research recommendation ('Investment in data infrastructure to monitor and respond to future shocks'), which is an external recommendation, not a national announcement.
answer.search_trail: 1) CAPMAS Central Data Catalog (censusinfo.capmas.gov.eg, T1): 629 studies overall, Agriculture collection 47 studies; data-access filter offers only 'Licensed data files' and 'Data not available'; login required — checked the Agricultural Property and Rein 2017 access-policy page, which sets confidentiality, access conditions and citation requirements rather than an open licence. 2) MALR Economic Affairs Sector database page (agri.gov.eg/databases/42, T3): plant-production query interface, dropdown years 2010–2019, empty result table in the retrieved page, no licence, download link or API documented. 3) MALR publications register (moa.gov.eg/publications, T3): 54 pages of PDF bulletins and studies (poultry, livestock, trade, food balance 2024) — documents, not datasets. 4) IFPRI/CGIAR policy note on remote sensing for Egypt (cgspace, T2): describes SPADE, a downloadable spatial agricultural database with over 1000 datasets/layers, and states that in Egypt only a fraction of collected datasets is made publicly available — used as corroboration of absence, not as the instrument. 5) ScienceDirect item was captcha-blocked and yielded no text. 6) A Hugging Face mirror of World Bank agriculture indicators for Egypt (T5) is a third-party republication of WDI aggregates, not an Egyptian open agricultural data instrument, and T5 cannot carry a statistic. No Egyptian national open-data portal page (e.g. a data.gov.eg agricultural catalogue) was among the retrieved sources, so no claim about one is made.

No published source I found states the **exact construct** “open agricultural data (machine-readable, AI-ready) for Egypt” as a single assessed measure.[2][13]

3.4.name: Digital land/plot registration

gates.reason: The indicator name 'Digital land/plot registration' does not resolve which of three registers is meant. The strongest operating evidence here is Egypt's economy-wide real-estate identification database (Law 88/2025), which covers all property types — urban apartments, factories, offices, vacant plots — and is explicitly NOT legal registration: the World Bank (reported second-hand at T5) stresses the property ID 'should not be confused with legal registration or proof of ownership', and that under 10% of Egyptian real estate is formally registered. Agricultural land is inside the law's scope (the Minister of Agriculture stressed linking the ID to agricultural land, noting fragmented inheritance), but nothing retrieved isolates agricultural plots or usufruct/holding records. The nearest evidence on the title-registration side is the Egyptian Survey Authority's national cadastre project (T3, 2018), which digitised cadastral maps and titles across governorate offices but is a general cadastre, not an agricultural register. No agriculture-specific digital plot register was found in the retrieved pages.

answer.value: Egypt has an operating digital property-registration infrastructure: Law No. 88 of 2025 (Official Gazette No. 24 bis, 17 June 2025) created a national electronic real-estate database assigning a unique unified national number to every property (land, buildings and structures), and MCIT reported in June 2025 that approximately 19 million national real estate identification numbers had already been issued across several governorates, alongside the earlier ESA/REPD national cadastre project that digitised 138,000 cadastral maps and 5.5 million titles.
